He is an Imperial pensioner, and is now in receipt of a pension of 40 cents or 50 cents every day of his life, and has been during the forty years he has been in Canada; and I am told, what I am glad to believe, that he is not in pecuniary difficulties, but is very comfortably off indeed. So I do not think his case is a bad one, and when we have increased his pay, I think we have treated him pretty well.
Hon. Mr. PRIOR, I am glad to hear the very good account the minister gives of Capt. Mackenzie, for I intended to bring up his case if my hon. friend the leader of the opposition had not done so. It seems a pretty hard case. He has served -in Persia and in the Indian Mutiny, and he says he did not come here on his own account, but was ordered here by the Horse Guards in 1866, and he is receiving now less than he did then. If the minister finds that he is in any pecuniary need, I hope he will take his case into consideration.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext:
I would like also to bring to the attention of the hon. Minister of Militia the case of the pay owing to Private Zong, a son of William Zong, of 29 Richmond street. Halifax, a member of the first contingent. He died, I think of enteric fever, in South Africa, and his father says that his pay from the 25th of October, Mr. BORDEN (Halifax).
1899, until the time of his death was never paid.
Does that mean the Imperial pay or the difference of pay ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext:
He does not state distinctly in his letter as to that; but I should gather from what he says that no pay whatever has been received during that time.
The	MINISTER	OF	MILITIA	AND
DEFENCE. The accountant says it is the Imperial pay.

The Canadian pay has been paid ?
The	MINISTER	OF	MILITIA	AND
DEFENCE. Yes.

It must be, then, the Imperial pay. Perhaps the hon. gentleman can take some	steps to remedy that ?
The	MINISTER	OF	MILITIA	AND
DEFENCE. I understand from the deputy minister that money is being forwarded from time to time, from the War Office to meet these claims, and that while he does not remember in regard to this particular claim, there is no doubt that in the very near future the money will be received and distributed through the Militia Department.

I was going further to state, with regard to this case as well as several other cases in my own constituency and in my own province, that we would be very glad indeed to know at as early a date as possible what the intentions of the government are with respect to making some provision or allowance in cases where soldiers who were killed or who died of disease in South Africa, have left persons in Canada dependent upon them. This was a matter which I brought to the attention of the government in the debate on the Address, and the right hon. gentleman who leads the government then stated that no definite announcement could be made at that time, for the reason that this government desired an exact statement of the intentions of the Imperial government, having regard to the terms of the despatch in pursuance of which the troops went to South Africa. That may afford a reason why no definite statement may be made at the present time; but I am sure there will be great satisfaction throughout the country, if an announcement of the policy of the government with respect to matters of that kind can be made at the earliest possible moment.
The hon. gentleman knows that in the cases of several men of the first contingent who were killed outright, some provision was made for their families by reason of a

certain insurance on their lives through Sir Charles Tapper. In my own constituency the families of two men who were killed at Paardeberg have received $1,000 each from the insurance. In the case of Private Zong, of ' H ' Company, that insurance was not available because he did not die of wounds but of disease. But the one case is as deserving of consideration as the other, and it is extremely desirable that the policy of the government should be placed before the country at the earliest possible moment.

I quite agree in the view just expressed. There are three sources from which assistance will be derived by the parties referred to. First, the Imperial government, which, in accordance with the original memorandum under which the contingents were sent to South Africa, agreed to give them Imperial pensions. Then there is a very large patriotic fund which has been used to relieve cases of distress, and in which there still remains an enormous sum that will be divided equitably among those entitled to share in it. Then there is this government, and I can assure the hon. gentleman that it is our intention to bring down a measure as will satisfy the requirements and meet what the most ardent admirers of the men who went to South Africa could desire. But I think it was prudent to wait until we were fully advised, and perhaps some conference may be had with the other two sources from which money will be derived to meet these obligations.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext:
Has the question presented itself to the hon. gentleman whether it would not be advisable, taking all the circumstances into consideration, to increase the pay given the men of the first contingent to an amount equal to that paid the men of the second and third contingents. I do not know whether the attention of the hon. minister has been drawn to that matter, but I know that I have been in receipt of communications asking me to draw his attention to it. There is a marked difference in the pay of the oflficers and men of the first contingent as compared with that of the second and third. While not desirous of making any comparisons, I think I am justified in saying that the men of the first contingent did exceedingly well and are entitled to the most liberal consideration, and I feel justified in bringing up this matter in view of the very satisfactory declaration which -the hon. minister has just made of the intention of the government to- deal liberally with those who served their country so well in South Africa. There is such a marked difference in the pay of the first as compared with the second and third contingents, that I hope the minister will give the matter his best consideration and ask parliament for an appropriation to make up the difference. I do not think that would take more than $100,000 or $125,000.
107*

The hon. gentleman must remember that when the Bill was introduced a year ago, under which the money was voted, the pay for sending these contingents to South Africa, this question of pay was very carefully considered. Without expressing any personal opinion-because I recognize that where all did so well it is undesirable that any distinction should be made, and the fact is recorded in history that it would be impossible to select one particular contingent which rendered more valuable services than another according to the opportunities presented-my hon. friend must not forget that when sending the contingents, the rate of pay of infantry was fixed at a certain amount and that of cavalry and that of artillery, and that the pay of the artillery and cavalry is considerably higher than that of infantry. Of course, if the House wishes to take a new departure and alter the law of last session, it is at perfect liberty to do so. But the fact remains that after careful consideration the rates of pay were fixed, and these men entered into a distinct contract knowing exactly what pay they would receive.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: Might I ask whether the same arms in each battalion get the same pay-whether the infantry, whether in the first or second or third battalion, gets the same pay, and likewise the cavalry and artillery ?
Yes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: I should be averse to any change. In the British and every other service the artillery and engineers are paid higher than infantry and cavalry.

What is the intention with regard to those members of the Canadian contingents who have enlisted for further service in South Africa ? There is a force of about 150 men, principally mounted rifles, who have re-enlisted. Is it the intention to recognize those men as a Canadian force, when pensions are being considered? Unfortunately in that small corps, the number of fatalities has been very much greater proportionately than in any other part of the forces which went out from Canada. These men might be debarred from consideration by a technicality, but certainlv those who re-enlisted for service in South Africa and who have rendered that service at such cost and risk are more entitled to our consideration than the members of the first three contingents who did not re-enlist.

I can quite understand the point of the hon. gentleman's plea. Technically our contract with these men has ceased, and this government was relieved of further obligation when they had served their full term and decided to enlist again directly

under the Imperial authorities. Now that the matter has been brought forward, I shall be glad to give it careful consideration. And, perhaps, after I have discussed the matter with any colleagues, I may be able to tell the House what we propose to do In reference to it. I would mot like to give an opinion at the present moment, though I agree with the hon. gentleman that these men deserve consideration from this country for the course they have seen fit to pursue.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: Might I also draw atten-ton to the fact that there are now on the way to South Africa something like 1,200 men. Although enlisted under Imperial authority, they are none the less Canadians. They go representative of Canada. We look to them to do for Canada what the first three contingents have done. I regret that they are not going as a fourth Canadian contingent. But, though not going as such nominally, they are such as a matter of fact ; and I would ask if it is the intention in any way to recognize them as Canadians in the matter of pensions in case of anything happening to them ?

The fact is-I do not know whether my hon. friend (Mr. Oliver) is aware of it-the pay that these 1,200 men are to receive from the British government, or from the colonial authorities ^n South Africa, is very large indeed. These men have seen fit to enlist for three years as a South African conskibulary of mounted police, at a rate of pay which is most genei'ous. I do not think that it will be necessary for us to consider the question that my hon. friend has put.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: What pay do they receive ?
I think six, seven and eight shillings a day for privates, and an allowance besides.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: The facts being as stated by the minister, I quite see that there is not the same necessity for considering these members of the South African constabulary as was to consider the members of the first, second and third contingents. But, I would merely ask if it is the intention of the government to give them recognition ? I think, it would be to our own credit to give these men recognition in some substantial way, although, possibly, not at the same rate as that provided for the men of the first, second and third contingents, who possibly made heavier personal sacrifices in order to go. I merely make the suggestion.
I take this opportunity to ask for information on a point referred to in a letter I have received-whether there

.
was insurance on the members of the-second contingent ? Sir Charles Tupper, as I understand, effected insurance on the members of the first contingent, ana some-thought upon the second contingent also, though I am told that that is not the case. I am requested to inquire whether there was insurance on the members of the second contingent. The letter is from friends of Dayton Brown Hammond, of Owen Sound, who enlisted in ' C ' Battery, Toronto, and left Halifax in February, 1900, and who was killed.
No, the government effected noinsurance whatever upon the members of any contingent.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: Am I correct in understanding that the insurance effected by Sir Charles Tupper was confined to members of the first contingent ?
So far as I know, yes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: Would the hon. minister be kind enough to explain about the army service corps, which we had touched upon when these other matters came up ? We understand pretty well the facts regarding the school of musketry, but the army service corps has not been explained.

It is proposed to establish, in Canada for the first time, a branch of the service, without which no army is complete, or able, in fact, to go into the field at all, known as the army service corps. This is a corps which shall have special charge of transport and supply. At present, it is intended only to appoint one officer, at a salary of $2,000, who shall be a member of the headquarters staff, and who shall organize throughout Canada, at the time of the camps, and in order to take part in the camps and get practical experience, a corps to be called the army service corps, to take up this important branch of the duties of the militia. This question was discussed two years ago, and a similar vote was then taken. But, for one reason or another, chiefly because of so many officers having gone away to South Africa, we did not carry it into effect then. Now we propose, after the 1st of July, to begin the organization of this important branch of the service.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: If it is in order at this stage, I would ask what is proposed to be done with regard to the organization of mounted rifles in Manitoba and the Northwest ?

Last year I stated in the House, in reply to questions, that we intended to

-organize a corps of mounted rifles in the North-west-to begin there, and, I hoped, later on, we might extend the organization "throughout the country at large. The proposal is as follows, though it has not been -carried into effect, although we are moving-in that direction : Military district No. 10 ; number of companies, 8. I thought I had the list of headquarters, but I see it is not here. I think there are four companies in the North-west. The organization is to be carried on at once.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: I have looked over the [DOT]different items under the head of militia, and I see nothing under which I could fairly discuss the question of the cadet corps of the various high schools of Canada. I would like to know from the hon. gentleman whether he intends to supply the cadet corps with the Lee-Enfield or the Lee-Metford rifles, or what encouragement he proposes to give to the various cadet corps.

It will be impossible at present to supply them with the Lee-Enfield rifles, but as fast as we are calling in the Martini-Henry, and the old Snider, we are issuing them to the cadets. We have only about 35,000 Lee-Enfield rifles at present in Canada, not more than enough to arm the active militia. It would, therefore, be impossible at the present moment to do more than we are doing.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: What about the Morris "tube ?
That is simply used for the purpose of practice; it is not a rifle, it is simply an attachment.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext:
I understand that in England the government gives the Lee-Metford arm, and valuable trophies are offered for public school comxjetition ; also the corps are allowed to compete in certain matches at Bisley. I understand now that the officer commanding military district No. 1 is in favour of the department adopting something of that kind in Canada. I also find in the report, Appendix No. 1 to the report of the Department of Militia, in a report of the Chief Superintendent of Stores, some reference that he makes to the cadet corps. He says :
The question of a suitable arm for issue to the cadet corps and boys' brigades, as also the [DOT]extent to which they are to be used for firing purposes or otherwise, ig" one which requires consideration, and the formulation of rules or instructions in connection therewith.
So it is evident the department is really considering this question. Then I find some mention made of the Morris tube :
The present supply of these articles will not admit of their being brought into general use
by the force. The necessity for their use during the winter months and in localities where rifle ranges are not available, is an admitted fact. Their use necessitates the provision of mantlets, which are the main expense. It is suggested that 100 mantlets and at least 200 aiming tubes, with 1,000,000 rounds of ammunition, be ordered for the present to commence with; this supply might afterwards be increased.
So I take it that the department is considering the advisability of doing this kind of thing. I understand there are something like thirty-eight cadet corps associated with the high schools, not counting others in the public schools, and having, I believe, an average of about fifty to each company. Those who are interested in the advancement of the cadet corps say that something like fifteen or twenty a year leave the various companies to follow other callings or professions ; they think these form a very good nucleus for the active militia, and that these young men, when they join the militia force, should be granted some rights that they have not now. For instance, I may give you what they recommend in that line ;
1.	That the government issue four Lee-Metford rifles to each high school cadet corps, and forty rounds of ammunition per member, with full permission to practice on the local regimental ranges on certain days of the week, or the issue of Morris tubes with targets and forty rounds of ammunition.
2.	That the government send to each principal of a collegiate institute having a cadet corps a copy of the general orders as they appear.	*
' 3. That each man who has been gazetted as an officer in a cadet corps, on joining the militia be held duly qualified for the rank of lieutenant.
4. That the government issue free of charge tents and blankets to any high school or collegiate institute cadet corps on requisition from the principal through the regular channel for instructional camp purposes, boards of education being held responsible for said stores, &c.
I remember that the late government, a few years ago, when asked to supply the various cadet corps witL tents, refused to supply them. Although I am not a military man, it occurred to me at that time that, considering the time these boys were giving for the purpose of drill, and for competition with each other in the various towns where these corps exist, it was not a step in the right direction. These organizations are imbuing our boys with a military spirit that will be in the interest of this country, if at any time we have trouble with any other country, and it seemed to me that instead of taking away any of their privileges, they should receive even greater encouragement. Speaking of the cadet corps in my own city, I may say that they have competed with London and other cities, and so far have succeeded in carrying off the prizes. They are very much interested in the work, and they have a good instructor, but they feel at present that the government is not giving them sufficient encouragement. We find that
34u3

in the Royal Military College of Kingston only twenty-nine cadets availed themselves of the privilege, under paragraph seventy-three of the Royal Military College regulations, of being attached to the Canadian militia at camps of instruction. I also find there are eight who have received commissions from the Imperial army. Now, this speaks well of the cadet corps. Though I do not pretend to be a military critic as to military movements and the like of that, yet, as a layman, I have compared the drill of the cadet corps with that of the 25th Battalion. While I do not wish to say one word against the efficiency of the 25th Battalion, I could not help remarking that, in my judgment at least, the movements that both organizations were put through were rather in favour of the cadet corps, these seemed to be better drilled, and they took a great pride iu it.

What the hon. gentleman has said is most interesting, and I may say that I am in thorough sympathy with his views. Unfortunately we have not the equipment, and I have no doubt that is the reason why my predecessor in a former administration found it impossible to comply with the request then made. We have to some extent been able to grant equipment in the past to some of the cadet corps ; but last year we had to give formal notice that we could not do it in future. If the whole militia of Canada are to drill annually, unless we get a very much larger vote than we are getting now, we cannot possibly supply the equipment outside the militia. But I quite recognize the importance of what the hon. gentleman has pointed out. These boys are the Canadian soldiers of the future, and they should be trained in boyhood, they should begin to-day, certainly as young as twelve years of age, and in that way we will make efficient and effective soldiers of them. I am entirely in sympathy with that idea. I am in hopes that it will be possible, by some arrangement with the provincial authorities, to have it made incumbent upon every teacher who receives authority to teach, to qualify himself as instructor at least in the rudiments of drill. I think it is something that may properly be done. I will try to make some arrangement with the different local governments by which this may be done. I was not able to catch everything my hon. friend said, but I will read, when it is published in ' Hansard,' carefully what he said. I will ask the general officer commanding and the headquarters staff to look into the matter. so that we may go as far as we possibly can with our present equipment and means to meet the views which he has given expression to.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext:
I have here the report of this cadet corps when it was in camp and Mr. INGRAM.
I will be very glad to turn it over to the hon. minister. He will find it a very creditable report indeed. As far as issuing the general orders is concerned, it strikes me there can be no objection to that.

In regard to the hon. minister's observations that he will take some steps to see that every teacher is qualified as a military instructor, I would ask him what he will do with the female teachers who are now employed in the proportion of about two to one of the men ?
I would like to ask the hon. minister who the two brigade majors are and where they are to be stationed.. The hon. gentleman said that part of the pay asked for was for two new brigade majors.
I may tell my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Prior) that we really need more than two. Toronto needs one and the other will probably go to Kingston.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: Have you not one at Toronto at the present time ?

No, only temporarily. Since Major General Herbert's time there have been no brigade majors. They were abolished at that time. But the work has increased so largely at our different district headquarters that it is absolutely necessary that the district officers commanding should have some assistance.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: Can the hon. gentleman say whom he is going to appoint as brigade major at Toronto ?
No, at the present moment I have not the slightest idea.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman
Carried.
I am afraid that I will have to ask the indulgence of the committee for two or three minutes notwithstanding the remarks of disapprobation which fell from hon. gentlemen opposite.
Go on.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext:
I intend to go on. I intend to refer to the question of the pay of the first contingent. It is so long since I left the militia force that I had forgotten that there is some difference between the pay of an infantryman, a cavalryman and an artilleryman. I do not say that the men of the second and third contingents got too much pay, but the difference between the pay of the men of the first contingent who were infantrymen and the men of the

second and third contingents was very great indeed. The pay provided for the men of the first contingent was forty cents a day.
Fifty cents.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: While the pay of the second and third contingents was half as much more.
Seventy-five cents.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: Why ?
I am not prepared to say why, but I think the difference is much greater than the difference in the pay between infantrymen, cavalrymen and artillerymen in the British service.
It is.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: I think I am justified in drawing the attention of the hon. minister to the fact and in asking him whether in view of the declaration which he made this afternoon as to the intention of the government to deal generously with these men who have done such good service for Canada and the empire, he should not take into consideration the advisability of increasing the pay all round of the men of the first contingent notwithstanding this difference that exists in the Imperial service between the pay of an infantryman, a cavalryman and an artilleryman, and make the pay of the men of the first contingent equal to the pay of the men of the second and third contingents. These men did not go as infantrymen particularly; they went out as volunteers. The men of the first contingent, if they had been competent to ride horses, would have gone as cavalrymen or artillerymen. They did not go for the pittance granted them by the government, but they went to give proof of their loyalty to Canada and to the empire. It seems to me, as it is a matter which would only involve an expenditure of $125,000 at the most, that it would be a gracious act on the part of the hon. minister to recommend and of his colleagues to bring down a proposition to pay these men of the first contingent an equal sum to that paid to the men of the second and tliii-d contingents.
Why was there this difference in the pay ? It was not only the difference between the different arms of the service.

No, that is quite true. The reason was this :	In the second contingent
a very large number, one of the regiments at any rate, a full regiment of cavalry, or of mounted rifles, was taken from the North-west mounted police whose pay was
seventy-five cents a day and it was felt that we could not diminish or reduce that pay. I was not quite correct in saying that it was cavalry and artillery pay, although I think that was the pay adopted for the officers, but, for the men it was North-west mounted police pay.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: But there were scores of men who were not in the North-west mounted police who volunteered to go as mounted infantrymen.
Certainly.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: I am not complaining that the men of the second and third contingents were paid seventy-five cents a day, but I am urging upon the hon. minister, that, in view of all the circumstances, it would be a graceful and proper act if the ministry could see its way to paying the men of the first contingent an amount equal to the pay of the men of the second and third contingents.

I will consider the matter.
Annual drilf, $275,000.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: I notice in the report of the general officer commanding, some remarks that come under the head of this annual drill. I see he again draws attention, as other general officers commanding have done in the past, to the inadequate time that is allowed for the annual training. I am rather disappointed to see that the hon. minister has not asked for a larger sum for the annual drill than last year, although I am quite aware that he had the whole militia training last year and he may have had some difficulty with his colleagues.
If you were in my place you would know.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext:
I know that. I see by the report of the general officer commanding that he has drawn attention to the short time allowed for the annual drill. He says :
Notwithstanding the most strenuous efforts on the part of officers, non-commissioned officers and men, these troops can never be made even fairly fit to take the field with the limited period of annual training that they receive under existing arrangements.
I am not going to say very much about that. This matter has been brought up time and time again. It does seem a pity, now that so much interest is taken in the militia which has acquitted itself so well, and now that it has been tried, that the government does not see fit to bring in a larger sum to bring the militia into a proper state of fitness to take the field. I see also,

that lie calls attention to the drill of city corps. He says :
So long as their training is confined to the limited area of a drill hall, with an occasional evening route march and a few church parades, it is obviously impossible for them to learn those most important duties of a soldier.
The most important duties of a soldier, in his opinion and in mine, are outpost duties, scouting, attack and defence of positions and the execution of hasty entrenchments. He does not say anything in regard to rifle shooting. I suppose that goes without saying. There is no doubt that city corps do not get sufficient drill in outpost duty, scouting and the movements that are in use in the field in warfare. The same report goes on to call attention to the musketry, but I referred to that before. The general does not say anything about the efficiency of ciry corps as to rifle shooting, but take the whole militia of Canada as a body it is certainly inefficient in rifle shooting. That is the reason why we are asking for more ammunition and more ranges. I am well aware that the minister is doing ail he can, but the government and the members of the House will have to be educated up to see the desirability and the necessity of giving greater assistance to the militia in the future than they have in the past.

Has the minister made inquiries from the different rural regiments particularly as to the possibility of the men being able to attend for sixteen days in camp ? If there is no difficulty in getting the men I certainly would urge very strongly the adoption of the opinion of the general in that respect. Sixteen days is quite a long time to get men away from their employment. After this year we will not have the South African war and other large expenditures to provide for, and I would suggest to the minister that when we have these large expenditures out of the way he should ask for the necessary money to carry out the suggestions of the general and place our militia in other respects on a satisfactory basis. As to the city battalions I believe it would be of great benefit to them if they would occasionally be sent into camp. The hon. member for Haldimand <Mr. Thompson) criticised the militia expenditures in the cities. I am personally in favour of a good round expenditure in the cities for the reason that city corps can be kept up efficiently in large numbers, and while my sympathies are in many ways more with the rural battalions, yet it is a good object lesson to have the city regiments turn out in fine military shape. There is more wealth in the cities than in the rural districts, and I understand that the officers and men themselves join in and do their share for the maintenance of the regiments in addition to the aid they receive from the government. While a handsome Mr. PRIOR.
uniform is not necessary to make a soldier yet nothing gives more encouragement than to see these regiments turn out well dressed on parade as it appeals to the eye and to the senses, and I am in favour of that if it can be done without any unreasonable expenditure.	.

I saw it stated in one of the city papars that No. 2 district will not be called out for drill until the fall, owing to the coming visit of the Duke of York. Has the minister reached a conclusion on that matter ?

The question has been raised as to whether the militia would prefer to postpone their annual camp until such time as His Royal Highness visits Canada, but no conclusion has been come to, and none will be come to without the general approval of the militia. As a military man, I have no doubt that we would get a great deal more good out of the money we spend if the camps were continued at least for four days longer. The expenditure for transportation has to be incurred anyway, and it would only necessitate the extra four days' pay and subsistence. For one reason or another we have adopted the rule of twelve-day camps, and probably one of the reasons wliy that term was adopted was that it was about as long as the men cared to be away from their homes and work. However, it is not impossible that the time might be extended. I would add that I do not believe that the money which is expended on the twelve days' drill is by any means wasted. I do not believe that the money spent on one man who goes to one camp and who does not go again is wasted. That man has learned valuable lessons which he will never forget. My hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Prior) has spoken of the amount of training necessary to enable the militia to take the field, and I would point him to the very work done by our contingents in South Africa. A large proportion of our men were not militia men. Many of them were men who never had the advantage of even one camp, and yet we saw how rapidly they became good soldiers. Even if we do not extend the time beyond the twelve days the money we expend on camps is doing very good work. I agree with the remarks made by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Tisdale) as to the city coxps. In case we were suddenly called upon to raise an army or part of an army in Canada we would of necessity have to rely for our first line of defence upon <the city battalions. These magnificent battalions are perfectly ready to take the field and the additional drill they require would be very quickly learned.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext:
I wish to bring to the attention of the minister the case of Pte. Sievert, of the first contingent, who

was nilled a t Paardeberg. I have in my hands statements made by two men who were in the line with Pte. Sievert at that battle, and I will read these statements to the hon. minister, so that he may consider whether or not any recognition of the very gallant act which led to the death of Pte. Sievert should be obtained. I do this because Pte. Sie-vert's father, who is one of my constituents, has discussed the matter with some of the officers in the Imperial service at Halifax, and they have stated to him, that it was a proper subject to mention to the War Office, or the Imperial authorities. I do not undertake to offer an opinion on the subject myself ; but, I give these statements of two men who were with Pte. Sievert at the time of his death. The following is the state-men of No. 7771, Pte. Laring H. Gates, ' F ' Company, Royal Canadian Regiment, dated September 2, 1900 :
I saw Private Sievert attempt to carry No. 7775, Private G. Orman, ' F ' Company, Royal Canadian Regiment, off the battlefield at Paardeberg on the morning of the 27th day of February, 1900, in the face of a brisk rifle fire.
We left our trenches at 2 o'clock a.m. to advance our trenches on to Cronje's position. Orman, Sievert and myself were in -the rear rank, which was fifteen paces in rear of the front rank.
We all had our rifles slung and carried entrenching tools. Private Orman was on my right and Sievert on my left. When the Boers opened fire we lay down. When the order came for us to retire we three got up together and started to retire. Orman was then about five yards on my left and Sievert was at about the same interval on my right. We had only gone a few yards when Orman cried out, ' I am shot and done for.' As soon as Sievert heard him cry, he started to go to him, and when he passed me I said to him, ' Where are you going?' He said, ' I'm going for Orman.' I told him, * You had better no-t, you'll only get shot yourself.' He said, ' I'm going to try at any rate.' He left me, and when he got almost to Orman he (Sievert) cried out, * I'm hit,' and he clasped his hand on his stomach and then fell down.
Silverton, S.A.R., Sept. 2, 1900.
(Sgd.) LARING H. GATES,
Pte., * F ' Company, R.C.R.
Witness :
H. B. Stairs, Capt., R.C.R.
That statement is corroborated by a statement of Pte. Wesley Irwin, a private in the same company, dated Halifax, December 17, 1900, as follows :
I saw Private Sievert attempt to carry No. 7775, Private G. Orman, * F ' Company, R.C.R., off the battlefield at Paardeberg on -the morning of the 27th February, 1900, in the face of heavy rifle fire.
We left our trenches at 2 a.m to advance on Cronje's position. Sievert, Orman, Gates and I were in the rear rank, which was fifteen paces in the rear of the front rank. We all had our rifles slung, and carried entrenching tools. When the Boers opened fire we all lay down, and when the order came for us to retire, we all got up together and started to retire. Almost immediately Orman was shot. Sievert at this
time was only six feet from me, and he at once started to bring Orman in, and was shot while trying to do so.
I brought this matter very briefly to the attention of the hon. minister last year by a letter, and he was good enough to send me in reply Col. Otter's report on it. Col. Otter seems to have thought that no action was advisable, because this very gallant act was not observed by the lieutenant in command at the time. Whether or not that is a good reason I do not know ; but I would like to bring to the attention of the hon. gentleman the fact that a similar gallant act. which resulted successfully, was mentioned by General Smith-Dorrien as good ground for recommending the Victoria Cross. I refer to his report on Pte. Kinsley, which is as follows :
No. 185, Private W. A. Kinsley, of the Royal Canadian Dragoons, in a most gallant way, carried out of action under a heavy and close fire, No. 172, Corporal Percy R. Price, of the Royal Canadian Dragoons, getting wounded himself in doing so.
It is true, in that case, that Pte. Kinsley was not killed, and his attempt was successful. In the present case, Pte. Sievert went to the assistance of Pte. Orman, who was a comrade of his-Orman came from Dartmouth, and Sievert from Halifax-and he was mortally wounded in doing so. Whether or not his act is capable of being officially recognized, I do not know ; but I do know that it was a very gallant act on the part of Sievert, one which makes us all feel proud of him as one of the Canadians who fought in South Africa ; and I do sincerely trust that it will be brought to the attention of the proper authorities, and that some recognition of it will be given.

I had hoped, when my hon. friend brought this matter to my attention, that Col. Otter would be able to throw some light upon it, and, therefore, I referred it to him. Unfortunately, as has been said, he does not seem to know much about it; but I have observed-and this would seem to support the view of the hon. leader of the opposition-that the commanding officer of Sie-vert's company, Capt. Stairs, distinctly states, in a letter which he addressed to Col. Otter, that Pte. Irwin would know the facts, and he adds :
I know of no one else who would know about it except Private Irwin.
From the statement which the hon. gentleman has read to the House, it seems that Pte. Irwin has a distinct knowledge of what took place.; and in view of that. I think it would be quite proper to submit this case, and I 'shall be very happy to do so. through the proper authorities, for the consideration of the War Office.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext:
I may say that the statement of Pte. Irwin was, I under-

stand, obtained through Capt. Stairs. I have the original statement in my possession, and I shall have very great pleasure in forwarding it to the hon. gentleman for the purpose mentioned.

House In committee on Bill (No. 70) respecting the E. B. Eddy Company.-Mr. Champagne.

I notice that in this Bill and the preceding one and several others introduced this session, there is a very bail principle. It seems to me that the aim of these companies is to obtain the power to get control of other companies in the same line and thus create a monopoly. If such a demand were made in the case of a railway Bill, the company would have to name the other companies with which it desires to amalgamate, and then it would be for parliament to decide whether it was proper to grant it this power. But in this case and the preceding one and others, powers are asked to amalgamate with any company in the same line, the object being to create a monopoly, which is against public interest.

Theoretically there may be something in what any lion, friend said, but we have to remember that the conditions with regard to trade and manufacture have changed very much in other countries. In England the power asked here is granted to a very large extent, in order to enable companies, by combining their capital and forces, to reduce the cost of manufacture and thus retain command in all the markets of the world. If in Canada we desire to hold our own in competition with other countries, we will have to grant the same power. Possibly for a short time, under some circumstances, this may have the effect the hon. gentleman fears, but there is greater likelihood of the public interest being protected by enabling strong companies to be formed out of combinations with other companies which, by means of the large capital at their command, will be able to reduce the cost of production and increase our trade. Take this particular industry, the manufacture of pulp into paper. Although it is claimed, and there possibly may be, a combine in the American republic and Canada, the price of paper has been reduced very considerably by the very fact that the uniting of Several companies into one with very large capital has enabled this article to be produced at a much lower cost than it was some years ago. There seems to be a misapprehension very often with regard to the granting of these Mr. BORDEN (Halifax).
privileges, which are asked for by legitimate commercial corporations. In this particular business, there is very little danger of the public interest being injured. While it requires large capital to establish a factory and purchase the limits necessary, on the other hand the area of limits is so large aDd our natural resoiurces so great that I do not think wrn need fear anything like a combine in this connection. By giving the opportunities to companies to acquire large capital and buy imprpved machinery we will encourage the investment of capital in this industry, which will increase its extent and give better employment to the people. .

The hon. gentleman says that theoretically my pretention may be correct, but practically it is not. The reverse is the case. This company is intended to have the power of generating light. This city is illuminated by electricity, and supposing there was another company which got its power from the Chaudiere Falls or anywhere in the vicinity to light this city, the company we are now incorporating would have the power to buy it up. And what would this company do ? The very first thing they would do would be to purchase the new company or amalgamate with it, and so do away with competition. In a great majority of instances, where these powers are applied for. we find it is not for the purpose of cheapening the product to the public, but for the purpose of making a monopoly. Railway companies have the same object in view when they amalgamate. We found by experience that when we gave charters to railway companies, the new roads were taken over by existing companies, and the public did not get the competition they expected. For years, therefore, we have sedulously avoided giving the power to amalgamate with any company unless that company is specifically named. If it is thought wise to give that power it is given, but not otherwise. I notice that we are departing from that salutary principle in private Bills. We had a Bill before the Banking and Commerce Committee this morning in which the same principle was introduced. Believing it to be wrong, I opposed that feature of it. as I oppose it in this case. Take the case of the electric railways, for instance. Look at the fight that was made year after year for the Hull road to get into Ottawa, and the fight made by the Ottawa company to prevent it. The Ottawa company have succeeded in getting control of the city for twenty-one years, and they are using it for their own purposes. They have never allowed the other company to get within the city limits. Their object was to prevent competition- and there is no competition at the present time. If this company required such a power as this for the legitimate purposes of their business, there would not be much hardship in waiting a few months-and it

need be only a few months-to give notice to the public in the usual way and apply to this House for the necessary power naming the company with which they wished to amalgamate. This course would have the advantage, that it would give the public three months notice to ascertain whether the power was to be used for a legitimate purpose or not, and, if not, to prepare to fight it.
It does not seem to mo that withholding this power from the company would affect the result. We know that at the present time companies are amalgamating without a line of legislation.
They cannot amalgamate without authority.
They can practically-one becomes a lessee of the other.
That is not amalgamation.
It is to all intents and purposes-it accomplishes the object the hon. gentleman seeks to provide against.
Then, what is the use putting in this clause ?

If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sproule) will permit me-the advantage of this is that it allows the company to do in a legitimate way what they can accomplish in another way. If they wish to take stock in another company, they can do it. We are only authorizing this company to amalgamate with the other company, but nothing can be done until the other company is specifically authorized to amalgamate with this company. I think it is better to give a clear charter to the company to do what they want to do, and do it in a legitimate way. And. as has been said by my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Sutherland), I do not see any reason why these companies should not amalgamate and make large concerns. Times have changed and the methods of manufacture have greatly changed. These companies must compete against much larger concerns than was the case fifteen or twenty years ago. We must consider these facts, and give companies powers that will enable them to compete effectually.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Wade) has shown tlie best reasons why this power should not be given. He says we should give power to do in a legitimate way what they would do anyhow. I suppose he means by that to give them power to do it in a legal and.proper way-in a way consistent with the law.
Perhaps it would be better to say, in an open way.

In an open way, then, to accept my hon. friend's correction of his
statement. Why should we give them power to do an objectionable thing in an open way, because otherwise they would do it in a hidden way ?
If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lancaster) will observe that I did not say that it was objectionable-not by any means.

I was saying that the answer made was no answer to the statement made by my hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule), that this was objectionable. If they have not this power unless we give it to them, the hon. gentleman's (Mr. Wade's) argument is no answer to the statement that the power should not be given. We ought to be very careful in giving such powers to the companies. The-reasons are very clear: they have been stated by my hon. friend from East Grey, so I shall not repeat his arguments. I think we should go into the matter more deeply than merely by saying there is no harm in giving this power, because the company can do as it wishes anyway. If that is so, we should not give them powers at all-leave them to the powers they have. But I think it is idle to say that this clause is wanted in the Bill, unless it is wanted on the theory that they have not the power unless we put it in. For the reasons given by my hon. friend from East Grey I think the power should not be given.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Wade) speaks of the railway companies having power to amalgamate, which is not the fact.
I said they could amalgamate without a line of legislation, and they are doing it every day.
The hon. gentleman must know as a lawyer that they cannot amalgamate. Leasing is one thing, amalgamation is another. If one leases the other they must come to parliament to have the lease ratified.
How about the New York Central ?

The New York Central is not a Canadian railway. I would ask the hon. gentleman (Mr. Wade) if he thinks there is no virtue in competition ? If not, why do we go on chartering and giving large bonuses to new companies to build lines to compete with those already in existence ? We have been doing that ever since confederation, and we are doing it now. If you allow them to amalgamate you defeat the object you aim at. I would ask the hon. gentleman also whether he thinks there is any injury caused by the monopolies we have in the country. Are not these companies taking exorbitant profits from the people for products that might be sold at much lower prices ? Are we not making

laws to control these monopolies and combines ? We have not yet been able to make an effective law, but we have not yet ceased trying. That being so. I do not see the advantage in giving this power. As soon as we get in sight of competition we find power granted indiscriminately to prevent competition. Now, if they wish to amalgamate, as I said, let them give notice to the public, and then come before parliament. If it is done otherwise, it is done in a way that is not generally known, and, when the public are looking for substantial benefits through competition, the companies amalgamate, and the public only wake up to a realization of what has happened when they find themselves faced by monopoly prices. We have what we are suffering from year after year, combines, and trusts, and amalgamations that are bleeding the people of this country to an extent that, I think, we ought to avoid as far as possible.

Where are these trusts ? I must admit, though I am a new member and come from a remote part of the Dominion, that I have not seen these great troubles that are complained against, resulting from any companies we have incorporated in Canada. On the contrary, I think the competition we have to fear is competition from the other side of the line where they are building up great systems, and we ought to be able to meet them. If we do not do that, we will be left, in my judgment. But 1 do believe that while the greatest latitude is given to these foreign companies, or rather while they are in a position to exercise the greatest latitude in the matter of combining, if we are going to put restrictions upon our own companies that we are organizing here, if we are going to put restrictions upon our capital, then I say we are putting our capital in an unfair position with regard to the competition on the other side of the line. We are likely to be the parties that would suffer from it. We are told to-day that we are going wrong, an attenmt is being made to frighten us by 4 combine ' and ' trust.' We have combines and trusts in existence, they originated upon the other side of the line, and we have got to meet that condition of affairs, and that is the reason why I take the stand that I do.
The hon. gentleman says that he doesn't know anything about troubles arising from combines. Does he know anything about the Standard Oil Company ?
I do.

Does he know that from the very day they got control of the oil refineries of Canada, oil has gone up ? Is he aware of that ? because every one else in the country knows it. Is he aware that we have a Bill before this House to-day to Mr. SPROULE.
legalize a deal between the province of Manitoba and the Northern Pacific Railway ? Why ? In order to get competition with the Canadian Pacific Railway. Is he aware that Manitoba is giving large bonuses to build that Rainy River Railway, and that we have given bonuses in this House, and the Ontario legislature also, in order to have competition ? Would it be an act of wisdom for us, after all this lias been done, to allow that company to unite with the Canadian Pacific Railway ? Why, we put clauses in Bills aiming to prevent companies uniting with the Canadian Pacific Railway, and then we are asked to destroy that competition that we desire to secure. That is the reason why we should avoid giving these companies the right to amalgamate. The hon. gentleman asks if we are going to prevent these people from putting themselves in a position to compete with others. I say no, not in a legitimate way. But when they desire to do so, all they have to do is to come to parliament and get the legislation that they require for that purpose, not for the purpose of effecting a combine and raising prices, but to meet unfair competition, and parliament is always willing and has never refused to allow them power to do that. Now, the hon. gentleman says that he does not know of any harm being done from combines anil trusts. Does he know anything about the agricultural implement amalgamations in our country ? Take the Massey-Harris Company, if yon like. In 1881, when they were burned out in the village of Newcastle, they applied to that small village for a bonus of 810.000 to start up their works. Without that aid they could not start their works, because they were too weak financially. The village was not large enough, and refused to give the aid. Mr. Massey then went west, and he managed by some means to effect amalgamation with another company with good capital and started in the west. A short time after that, another company that appeared in competition was destroyed, up went the jirice of implements, and it has been up from that day to this; and practically to-day the implement manufacturers of the country are nearly all under one understanding with regal'd to prices, and the farmers have to pay, and cannot help themselves. I say that the farmers of Canada are being bled white to-day in consequence of these companies having combined. 'Take the Massey-Harris firm to-day. They commenced business for the second time in 1882, and they have made so much money since that that firm has given away over $5,000,000. we are told, for philanthropic purposes. Where does it coime from ? It comes out of two lines, it comes out of the labour that does the work and for which they pay lower wages than they ought to pay. and it comes out of the farmers to whom the implements are sold at a higher figure than is just. It is to

avoid this painful result that we should strive in this House. As long as any company comes before this House for legislation to enable it to facilitate its business, and proves that it will not resort to an amalgamation which will result in increasing the price to the consumer, or that it will result in reducing values, there would not be the slightest objection to granting such legislation.

The hon. gentleman asked if X knew the Standard Oil Company. I have had occasion to know something of it in different ways. In one way I know of it from a pamphlet that was issued by the hon. gentleman and his friends just before the last election. X believe it was intended for Ontario consumption, but it got down into the province of Nova Scotia. In that pamphlet we were told that the price of kerosene oil was increased, because the present government permitted the Standard Oil Company to import their oil in tank vessels. That was one of the arguments that was used. I am not prepared to accede to the position taken by the hon. gentleman that the Standard Oil Company has increased the price of kerosene oil here.
Every one knows it.

Well, I do not know it. I am willing to be convinced, but I have never heard any argument to satisfy me, though I have heard a great many arguments upon this subject. Now, with regard to the Massey-Harris Company. I know that before they were in existence the price of agricultural implements in Nova Scotia was much greater than it is at the present time. I know that since these concerns have been placed in a position w'here they can compete with those of the other side of the line, because they have sufficient capital for that purpose, the price of agricultural implements has been reduced. That is my experience so far as the province of Nova Scotia is concerned. I am astonished the hon. gentleman cannot see that if there is a concern upon one side of the line employing two or three million dollars, and if it comes into competition with a firm or company here that is only permitted to employ some $200,000, the disaster must be to the smaller company ; and it is for that reason that I have contended that our companies shall be given the same powers that are given to the companies upon the other side, that they should have the same jiowers of employing large capital as they have upon the other side of the line. But when it comes to appear that these trusts or combinations, as we call them, are not in the interests of the public, then it is time to have legislation for the purpose of controlling them, but surely that legislation should not prevent these companies from legitimately competing with those upon the other side of the line.

We are somewhat embarrassed by the fact that this very privilege, almost in the same words, has already been given to another company of a like character, and it would certainly seem a little awkward to give it to one and to refuse it to the other. Nevertheless we must deal with the principle involved in the legislation. I do not share the alarm which some people feel as to the creation of large corporations. I think large corporations are necessary for doing business under modern conditions, both here and across the line; nor do I object to this company being a large company. But what I do say is that if any company wants to amalgamate with another company it is the business of parliament to say whether it shall be allowed to do so, in' the light of the particular circumstances which may then be disclosed. I do not approve of this practice of giving powers to companies to amalgamate with any other company with which they may wish to amalgamate. The proposed amalgamation may be wise, may be in the public interest, may be designed to bring about these economies in management which are in the public interest; but I think parliament should reserve the right to judge of that case in every instance that it should be asked to give power to amalgamate with a particular company, and not to give a general power, which I regret to see parliament seems inclined to give.
Bill reported, read the third time, and passed.

House in committee on Bill (No. 57) to incorporate the Crow's Nest Southern Railway Company.-Mr. Galliher.
On section 12,
I thought this was the Bill that the government had an amendment on to prevent discrimination in the sale of coal and coke to the Americans as against the people of British Columbia.

Yes, this is the Bill, but the hon. gentleman (Mr. iSproule) is mistaken in assuming that the Bill was to be amended. The matter, as presented to the committee, was not that the Bill should be amended but that before the Bill should be finally passed, an agreement which was laid before the committee should be signed by the several companies. It was not contemplated that it should form part of the Act. Such was the understanding before the committee, whether the hon. gentleman understood it so or not.
speakername: The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Hon. W. S. Fielding).

speechtext: I was not before the committee.

There were some objections to putting a clause

into tliis Bill for tlie reason that the bodies which control the coal mines and the proposed railway, although they are the same set of men, are two corporations and it was held to he difficult to legislate as respects the railway company when the company to which we wished to apply the prohibition was the coal company, and because, even though they might be the same set of men, they were two distinct corporations. It was therefore proposed that the difficulty should be overcome by an agreement to he signed by the government on the one part, by the coal company on another part, and by the railway company on the third part, such agreement to be to the effect that in the event of any attempt to discriminate against the consumers of coal or coke in Canada, either on the part of the railway company by its rates, or on the part of the coal company by its prices, or by the two companies, then the Governor in Council might by order place restrictions upon the power of the railway company to carry coal and that after the passing of such an order, if coal or coke should be sold or carried by these companies in violation of the spirit of the agreement, they should become liable to a penalty of $3 per ton for every ton of coal or coke so carried. That is, in brief, the substance of the agreement which was finally come to. The government can execute the agreement at once through its ministers, the coal com-* pany can execute the agreement through its proper officers, but the railway company could not execute the agreement as they have no corporate existence until the passing of this Bill. It was thoroughly understood between a committee of the government and the promoters of this Bill that before the Bill was finally passed that agreement would he executed by the coal company and by the gentlemen who are the promoters of this railway company. There was a full understanding that unless that agreement is signed as agreed, this Bill will not pass to its third reading in this House.

I want to say in connection with this Bill, that I did not attend the committee at the last consideration of it. I was there the first time. But, the information was given that such an agreement would he desirable. It seems to me, from the information we get through the press regarding the agreement, that it may be worthless and for this reason : while the coal company and the railway company, which are practically the same parties, may enter into that agreement with the government, the government have power to punish them in the event of violating the agreement; by selling the coal south of the line cheaper than in British Columbia. I do not see any provision in it that they must give a full supply to British Columbia before they export. Whether that is in it or not I do not know. But, the feature of the Mr. FIELDING.
agreement that attracted my attention is the disability which rests on the Canadian Pacific Railway to develop their coal lands. They entered into an agreement with the coal company not to develop their coal lands for a certain number of years until the coal company got theirs well under way. Until that disability was lifted this bargain would remain in force, hut just as soon as that was removed then the bargain became null and void. It seems to me that this agreement would be practically worthless, because you give them the power to commence negotiations with the company and they will do as will likely be done by tbe Eddy Company to wbicb we gave power tonight. As soon as another party starts operation they will immediately get control of it, and the agreement is null and void. The agreement to have any value should give the control to the government for all time.

I might set the hon. member (Mr. Sproule) right in that respect. That was the agreement as it originally stood. I, with some others, mentioned the fact that if competition arrived at such a stage as not to require these restrictions, then, if these restrictions were taken off, they might buy up the other companies and get a monopoly. The agreement was amended to state that it might be suspended ; not declared null and void, but may be suspended when competition reaches such a stage that it is not necessary any longer to enforce these restrictions.
I think they should he kept all the time.
It is not rendered null and void ; it is simply suspended.
Do I understand that the same agreement may be called into existence at any time ?
Yes, the enforcement of it may be 'suspended.
In any event, they will not enforce it unless there is need to. -I understood that the agreement became null and void. That was in the papers.
The papers were not right.

It is amended as stated by the hon. member (Mr. Galliher).

I would ask that the third reading be fixed for another day, when we shall have a clear understanding that the agreement is signed.

Militia-Annual drill, $275,000.
['That is all. But I do not think the amendment covers the ground that I desired to have covered by the section prepared by the law clerk.']

I see that the general officer commanding in his report advises an increase of pay, as mentioned by the hon. member for Hahlimand (Mr. Thompson) this afternoon. On page 35, he draws attention to the fact that at the present time there are a large number of recruits every
i year, that many men do not come out for I drill year after year, even although they do not get their discharge, and that the desertions amount to about 25 per cent of the whole militia. That is a very serious state of affairs. I know that a great many men do not look on the matter with the gravity that they should. They think when they sign that it is only a matter of form, and that they can turn up at drill or not just as they please. I do not go so far as to say that they should all be summoned ; but I have seen a few hauled up before the police magistrate and fined, and it has had a most beneficial effect. I think there ought to be some means thought out by the Militia Department whereby men would be shown that when they sign for three years they are expected to turn up and do their proper duty. It is a most unfortunate state of affairs that they should look on the oath which they take and the document they sign as so much waste paper. It is to be regretted that, after all the expense in training these men, so many of them, after they are partly trained, should go away, and the country get no further benefit from their services.
The general officer suggests that the pay of the private militiaman should be increased according to service-50 cents the first year, 60 cents the second year, and 75 cents the third, thereby giving some incentive to the men to put in their full three years drill. And afterwards he suggests that the men should be encouraged to continue in the service. He says :
And I would further strongly recommend that on the expiration of their three years engagement, men of good conduct and especially noncommissioned officers, be encouraged to continue in their service on annual attestations not exceeding six years in all, receiving a gratuity on the conclusion of each extended year's training.
That suggestion is well worthy of consideration. If that could be worked out to a successful issue, it would be the means of greatly strengthening the militia and keeping good men in the ranks.
On page 39 in the report of the adjutant general, there is a paragraph regarding canteens. This is a question which was brought up last year and the year before, and caused a good deal of discussion in the press and the country generally. I think that this paragraph in the report should be seriously considered :
(6). We have heard a great deal during the past few years about the sale of liquor in camps. While I do not think that strong alcoholic drinks should be permitted, I am unable, after an experience of many years with the Canadian military forces, to advocate, or understand how well-intentioned people can advocate prohibiting the sale of lager beer and soft drinks. That men who have performed hard training in the heat of the day should be obliged to quench their thirst with lukewarm water conveyed to the grounds through half-exposed pipes, or in open-headed hogsheads, and thus exposed to impurities, seems to me to be most unreasonable. If men

34 24
are able to obtain soft drinks and lager beer instead of being compelled to drink impure or nauseating water, it would have the effect of restraining them

Here is the pith of the whole thing :
-from seeking stronger drinks outside the camping grounds, and from bringing liquor into camp in bottles, and thus temperance might better be promoted.
I am heartily in accord with that opinion, and X think that every officer, who has had much to do with camps, must see its force. Men who are in the hahit of taking any kind of drink all the year round are not going to do without it, if they possibly can get it, when they are in camp, doing hard work under a hot sun-and putting in training under energetic officers is hard work. If they cannot get it in the canteen, they will get it outside, and the liquor they will get outside, especially where it is sold close to the camps, is not likely to be the best kind, and the men are likely to take more than if they could get it in a legitimate manner in the canteen. I do not say that spirits should be sold, but nobody could possibly object to lager beer and soft drinks. This subject is well worthy the attention of the minister, and although he has time and again declared that he was not going to allow any liquor to be sold, I think that, in view of the strong representations made to him by men who are competent to judge, he should reconsider his decision.

I feel it my duty to endorse what my hon. friend has just said. I know that a large section of the community entertain very strong opinions on what they call temperance. I believe in temperance, but temperance does not mean that a man shall not drink beer. I am emphatically in favour of prohibiting the use of spirits in the canteen, but I must endorse the suggestion contained in the adjutant general's report with regard to the sale of lager beer and soft drinks.
I believe also that the suggestion of increased pay for each additional year's service is a good one. The pay is small enough anyway, and it would be well to try the experiment of increasing it each year.
Coming back to the subject of the' canteen, I must say that after an experience of fifteen years in camp, and commanding a regiment, I have come to the opinion that there is nothing more conducive to keep the men in camp than a canteen where lager beer, soft drinks, cigars, &c., will be sold. This will please them just as well as going into town, where not only they will meet their fellow soldiers from other regiments, but also well-meaning, but injudicious people, who often induce them to drink more spirits than they should, and often more beer than they should. True, temperance does not consist in trying to prevent people from getting liquor of any kind, but in furnishing them with the most harmless Mr. PRIOR.
drink possible, and in seeing that they drink only in moderation.

I have generally been opposed to this policy of playing at war and military life. I think that it has a tendency to draw from industrial pursuits many young men who would be otherwise more profitably employed. But like many others, my mifid has become somewhat changed on this question of military policy. I have been many years against the expenditures on military matters and against lengthening the time of drill, but I do think that the suggestion of the major general with regard to increasing the pay each succeeding year, is a wise one. I have watched the course of military events for many years in the locality where I reside, and I have usually found that our young men, after they had served two or three years in camp, and just about the time they began to be somewhat proficient, dropped out, and one of their reasons is that the pay is entirely insufficient to induce them to remain longer. By gradually increasing the pay, they would be induced to remain longer in the force, and thus our militia would be considerably improved.
As regards the canteen, I have not much to say. I notice considerable feeling against it, not so much because people believe that lager beer or the ordinary ale is so injurious, as because they believe that if these liquors be sold, whisky will also be smuggled in, I am not so much afraid, however, of the danger of thus destroying our young men by the occasional use of a few glasses of ale or lager beer, as some people are. I do not think that lager beer or common ale is very injurious if drunk in moderation, so long as they drink nothing stronger. But the real danger, of course, consists in allowing the sale of spirituous liquors, which is usually done when ale or lager beer is allowed to be sold.

I fully endorse the views expressed with regard to increasing the pay of the militia in camp by grading it in the way advised by the major general, namely, giving an increase each year of service. That would induce our young men to continue in the service, whereas at present many of them enroll the first year and drop out the second or third. Now, there is another matter to which I would call the attention of the hon. minister, a very important matter and one that has not been touched upon. The main object of the hon. minister must be to have every one who is enrolled in the militia an efficient officer or soldier. And how is that to be accomplished ? There is only one way, and that is to have military instruction and drill made a part of the education of the youths of this country. I am fully aware that the minister has not complete control in this matter, for education is In charge of the provincial

authorities. But he can advise the local governments that they instruct their educational officers, the superintendent of education and each of the inspectors to require that military drill be taught in the public schools. If that is done, the children null bo inspired with military ardour and zeal in the interests of the service, and every one of them thus taught will be good loyal citizens. Youthful impressions are very lasting, and in the words of the old proverb : train up a child In the way he should go, and when he is old he will not depart from it. One who is trained on soldierly lines in youth will become a soldier in reality. I do not say that the hon. minister should go to the expense of giving the schools the Lee-Enfield rifle or the Oliver equipment-these, perhaps, will be more useful in the hands of militia men. But the hon. minister has a lot of obsolete equipment that can be placed at the disposal of the schools-the academies, higher schools at first to have the supply, and as the complement of obsolete arms and equipment in store grows greater, he can supply the smaller schools also. The children will be pleased to see the racks in their schools, because they would be a sort of ornament as well as being designed for use. Then, instead of occupying their spare time in mere racing about or perhaps in idle rude play, let them be drawn up regularly as soldiers and engaged in drill. Let them have 'their officers as soldiers do-their colonels, majors, adjutants, captains and non-coms-without, of course, the commission. This will give them a certain amount of inspiration and rivalry, each one to rise in the ranks. Nor should this Instruction be confined to the boy youths alone-let it be given to the girls as well. Let them have a separate drill, apart from the boys. I feel satisfied that the training thus brought about will be of immense advantage to them. It will give them fine physique, beautiful and easy carriage, graceful manners and a martial bearing.

They have that now.
iMr. KAULBACH. They are supposed to have it, and many of them have, but there are exceptions. They have this system in Germany and there is no reason why we should not adopt it in Canada. With such a system, every youth, when he arrives at the age of sixteen, will feel himself fully equal to meet the requirements of the soldier with very little training. When he goes to camp, he will easily become a well-drilled soldier, and need not go into the awkward squad. This is the ground-work of the success of the militia service, and I feel satisfied that it is a step iu the right direction. I hope the hon. minister will accept the view I have here suggested and will communicate with the local governments and let them make the necessary arrangements to see that the idea is carried into effect.
