Surely the hon. gentleman (Mr. Kaulbach) was not speaking seriously. But, in case he was serious, I desire to say a word so that, sitting near him, I may not be supposed by my silence to endorse his sentiments. Surely, he does not ask us to take our little children from their games and train them in the arts of war. Our little children ! that is surely a most outrageous proposition. He gave us the proverb of training up a child in the way he should go, and how did he apply it ? Let us train up' the children in the arts of war, train them to be colonels and captains, train them to fight among themselves, and they will fight when they get older. Surely, we are not going to have that sort of thing in Canada. So far as our militia is concerned, we want to do away with the glamour, the tinsel, the show of it. It is necessary that we should have a militia force, but let us make it democratic, encourage our young fellows to have that patriotism that will make them feel that to them we look as defenders of the country, and that to defend it properly they must learn something of the art of war, mainly -they must learn to shoot. It is not the right-about-turn and so on, the mere drill and mechanical movements that we need to teach our children. If the Boer war has taught us anything, it has taught us that men from farms, men untrained, if they can shoot, are good soldiers, and that mechanical soldiers are not the ones who can win battles in our day. I did not intend to take any part in this discussion. But when I hear an hon. member seriously-I believe he was serious-advising that we should take our young children away from their play, give them guns and bayonets and drill them as soldiers
They will like it better than any play.

That may be my hon. friend's (Mr. Kaulbacli's) opinion, but it is not mine, and I have the right to hold and to express my own opinion. I do earnestly protest against this being taken as the sentiment of this House. At any rate, for my part, I must dissent from it. I protest against trying to make out that we in Canada are a military people. We are not a military people, we are a democratic people, but not for that reason the less loyal or the less patriotic.

I have no *desire to create a jingo spirit amongst the people of Canada, but I wish to see our Canadian boys so trained that, should occasion arise that when they were called upon to defend our country they will be able to do *so with success. To do this they must be taught from their youth. We heard this afternoon that a new mode of warfare has been developed. WTe find that drilling in battalions, which my bon. friend; from Victoria would advocate, is of very little use



nowadays. A man must learn to slioot and shoot straight ; he that can do that best is the best soldier. We must teach our boys to shoot, but first, we must teach them discipline. And 1 may tell my hon. friend from Lunenburg (Mr. Kaulbach) that an the province of Ontario our people have uot much of the jingo spirit, but they are teaching their children how to drill, and I thins that that is what our school teachers, even our school ma'ams must teach.
I am proud to see the spirit that is arising amongst our young people, in Ontario at least, in order that they may be able to defend themselves when the time shall arrive. The government should encourage this sxairit by training them properly how to march and how to shoot. I think that is the object this government has in view, so that within a few days, if the need should arise, we may have 200,000 young fellows ready to fall into line. If the people of other countries knew that, they would hesitate before they attacked us. I want to. say a word also with regard to the question of a canteen. I am not going to advocate a canteen. If these young men have been properly trained at home by their mothers and by their fathers to leave liquor alone, and if it is known that when they go out to drill there will be a canteen where they can get soft drinks, as the hon. member for Victoria calls it, or where they can get liquor, their parents may hesitate to encourage their boys to go to these military drills. I believe that men who do not touch liquor are far healthier and can march further in a day. General Wolseley, who was lately commander-in-chief of the British army, when he was in this country, marched 4,000 Canadians up to the North-west, and they did not have a drop of liquor, and he did not lose a man. My hon. friend from Victoria (Mr. Prior) might not be able to do that. I would not like my boys to join a contingent where there was a canteen of soft or hard drinks put under their nose. I think our young men do not require it. Plenty of excellent water can be found, and if you give them plenty of good food I do not think they need a canteen.

I hope the opinion expressed by the hon. member for Winnipeg (Mr. Puttee) is not the opinion that prevails in that great western country. For my part I am a man of peace, when peace can he maintained with dignity; but I think that war is the noblest employment of mankind when waged in defence of right. A nation that is not prepared to fight at any moment, a nation that has a man, woman or child, who is not prepared at any moment to fight in defence of their own country, is not worthy the protection of a government. The one thing which is creditable in the history of the Boer war is the fact that every Boer man, woman and child is prepared to sacrifice his or her life in defence Mr. ROBINSON (West Elgin).
of their country, a country that was not a glorious country or with glorious traditions in any sense, but still they are prepared to fight for their country. That is the most creditable thing that can be said about that awful oligarchy. Sir, I have been delighted to see in my own part of this Dominion a splendid military spirit growing up among our people, an aggressive military spirit, a spirit that gives a basis for high and dominant feeling. No nation is worth anything where a high and proud feeling does not characterize the whole people. After forty years of adherence to a proud and noble policy, the British Empire adopted a cowardly policy; and I was glad the other night to hear some hon. gentleman revile the British government for the miserable conduct they exhibited a few years ago in giving away that splendid territory in. Maine; and 1 hope that if ever the mayor of Ashburton appears in Canada, some man will horse-whip him from end to end of the country. I am an Imperialist of the strictest sect of the Imperialists, and, Sir,
I cannot characterize with sufficient contempt the policy of the British government for forty-five years. Every nation in the world stole her territory and insulted her, and down to the incident of Fashoda the British spirit never came back. The British nation, after they waged their great war with Napolean, that splendid and magnificent captain, the peer of all the greatest captains of the world, after they waged that war for twenty-two years, then up rose a weak race of demagogues, after 1830, after two generations, the British race has become decadent. After two generations they stood by and saw the ancient glory of that empire, which had been won by a succession of magnificent generations, thrown to the winds. Thank God, however, there are other British nations growing up in Australia, and in Canada, and in Africa, that will take a hand in the discussion of her foreign policy. I stand here to claim that from this moment when there is any weakness shown in any British cabinet with reference to her foreign policy, every Canadian in this House of Commons, every man in the House of Commons of Africa- which I hope will be established as a consequence of this war-every member of parliament in Australia, shall rise and demand that they have as much to say about the foreign policy of this empire as the British people. Why, Sir, a man born in London, stupid and ignorant, has more to say about the foreign policy of the British Empire than educated Canadians. Why, Sir, one Canadian has more horse-sense and more intelligence than a thousand Englishmen wrapped together. Now, when it comes to a discussion of the proper policy to follow,
I claim as much right as any man in the hall of St. Stephen's to discuss the foreign policy of this empire, and to settle it upon high and dignified lines, characteristic of the Bri-

tisli race for a thousand years down to 1830, when that period of disgrace and meanness began for the whole British people.
Now, I want to say a word or two with regard to the canteen. 1 do hope that the hon. member for Victoria, B.C., will not be able to allure the Minister of Militia and Defence .into establishing the canteen system so far as Nova Scotia is concerned. 1 understand the minister is rather popular with the ladies in my province, but I undertake to say that if he establishes a canteen in that province the mothers and sisters of Colchester will warn him never to set foot in that country. I quite agree with the hon. member for West Elgin (Mr. Bobinson) that it would be a disgrace ai the present time, when the whole world is moving towards the abolition of the canteen, to have it re-established in Canada. Why, Sir, Kitchener's army that captured Khartoum was a thoroughly teetotal army. There was no canteen, it was abolished when the soldiers began to march. In the United States navy, previous to actual battle, the canteen is abolished in order that the highest nerve and the highest qualities of the soldier, and the seaman, may be exhibited in the face of the enemy. Now, when the whole trend of military discipline is towards the abolition of the canteen, I want the Minister of Militia and Defence- because I am a Liberal upon this subject- to learn that so far as the maritime provinces are concerned, the sentiment of that people, the best educated people, is overwhelmingly against the canteen. I quite agree with the sentiment that no mother or no father will permit their boys to go into a militia camp if you are going to have the drunken orgies that are inseparable from the canteen. I quite agree with the hon. member for Victoria, B.C., that there may not be any harm in a glass of lager, but when you have a canteen, the drinking of that and stronger liquors will inevetiably take place with the consequent demoralization. I have always said that the ultimate political destiny of this continent was in Canada. Why, in fifty years hence the centre of political power on this continent will have been transferred from Washington to Ottawa. More than that, if we want to have a strong and powerful people here, we must have a trained teetotal people. I became a teetotaler because I am an Imperialist, because I believe to be an Imperialist you want to have the highest citizenship and the teetotaler exemplifies the highest citizenship in this country. He is healthy and he can endure provided he is not soaked in wine or liquor. Because I am an Imperialist and a teetotaler I oppose the re-establishment of the canteen. I want the hon. minister not to be entrapped by any of these appeals that we have Beard in regard to the improvement of the militia of this country.

My hon. friend from Winnipeg (Mr. Puttee), it seemed to me, scarcely did justice to my hon. friend from Lunenburg (Mr. Kaulbach), and I must say that I dissent entirely from the views which were expressed by the hon. member for Winnipeg. I do not think that he succeeded in correctly presenting his real views to the House. My hon. friend must not forget that all we are inculcating and teaching in this country is the necessity of defence. My hon. friend has referred to the encouragement and fostering of the patriotic spirit. I would like to know what better way there is of encouraging a patriotic spirit than by teaching our young boys the importance of defending their country, and that their country is worth defending. I would like to point out to my hon. friend and this committee, that it does not follow that in the money we are expending annually and by the pains we are taking to teach dril. to our young men, we are inculcating a warlike or quarrelsome spirit. It is nothing of the kind. What we are teaching is, that we have a magnificent country, that we are an independent, self-respecting people, and that it is our duty to defend ourselves from the attacks of any one who may exhibit a desire to take this country away from us. Surely, if this is sound, the sooner we attempt to teach it to our boys in the schools the better it will be for us.
Two other matters have been the special subject of discussion. The first was in reference to the pay, which was referred to by my hon. friend from Victoria, B.C. (Hon. Mr. Prior), by the hon. member for South Norfolk (Mr. Tisdale), and others, and which was dealt with in the report of the major general. I think there is a good deal of force in what the major general has said, and I shall feel inclined to give his recommendation a trial. However, I do think that the adoption of his recommendation would not have the effect of bringing back to camp for a second or third year all the men who have gone out the first year. If it would have the effect of inducing a large percentage to return, it is certainly worth trying, although it would involve some additional expenditure. I think, as the hon. member for Victoria has pointed out, that our volunteers do not correctly apprehend their responsibility after enlisting. They do not look upon it as desertion, and I think if we took pains to let them thoroughly understand what the true position of affairs is, and what their responsibility is after having signed the roll and entered into a contract to go out for three years, it might have a good effect, and that, perhaps, some arrangement could be made to improve the existing condition. The existing condition to which the major general referred is not worse than it was two years ago, or five years ago, or ten years ago. It is probably not so bad as it was then. I think that this

year we will endeavour to instruct captains to issue a formal notice, which will he served upon the men some time before the camp, to, if possible, secure a larger attendance than in the past. The general lias suggested that something of this kind should be done, and we are now taking steps to see that it will be done, and I hope to be able to report, after the drill of this year, that this evil has not existed to the same extent as it has in the past. There is no doubt, too, that the man to whom we pay 50 cents the first year is a better man, and is worth more to the country, the second year, and we might very well afford to pay him an additional amount. This would be quite true of the third year. He will be worth more. If he cnooses to go on after that, because we want to bring in new men after the three years, we might keep on for a term of years the increased rate of pay.
In reference to the canteen ; this is a somewhat delicate question, but, I am bound to say that I think the militia could get along very well in camp without the use of intoxicating liquors. I am inclined to agree with the hon. member for West Elgin (Mr. Robinson) that cold water is not too bad a thing. When the hon. gentleman referred to Wolseley's historic march from eastern Canada up to the Red river, as it was called in those days, I remembered having read a series of articles published in Blackwood's magazine by Gen. Wolseley, who was then Col. Wolseley, describing the hardships of that march, and I remember that he said that he had learned a lesson from the hardy lumbermen of Canada, and that nothing was used on that march stronger than tea. He believed that there was nothing which would restore a tired and weary man as well as tea. He considered it infinitely 'superior to the grog which used to be issued to the British soldiers. There is a misapprehension as to the meaning of the word canteen. The canteen does not necessarily mean a place where liquor is sold. Canteens contain everything that is necessary to the comfort of a soldier, tobacco, cigars, soft drinks, such as ginger ale, and anything of that kind, and all sorts of articles that he may require. The canteen still exists, but we have passed regulations to exclude from it alcoholic liquors. Such liquors as ginger ale, soda water, and that sort of thing- buttermilk-some one says, are not excluded from the canteen, and will not be excluded. While personally I do not suppose that there would be any serious injury in a moderate amount of lager beer, still, I do think that there is such a strong feeling, as has been said, among the mothers and daughters and sisters in this country of the young men whom we want to go into camp, that we would find that if we were not pretty particular and pretty careful in this respect, that prejudice, that feeling-perhaps Mr. BORDEN (KinfeJs).
it is not right to call it a prejudice-would have a very considerable effect in interfering with the success of our camp. So far as I am concerned, I have been attending a camp for many years from which liquor has been excluded. I will not say that there never has been liquor drunk there, but it is against the rules of the camp, and it is not sold in the canteen. I believe that the condition of that camp is better than it was in the days when liquor was sold.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: It is not true that in military camps where spirits are prohibited according to the regulations, where a canteen exists, that in defiance of the regulations, they have spirits in the canteen. I trust the mernuer for Colchester (Mr. Gour-ley) will not repeat it again until he has better evidence for liis statement. It is unfair to the commander of the camps, to the commanding officers of the battalions, and to the officer of the day, to say that a canteen exists where it is prohibited. I agree with the hon. minister that there is a strong feeling against the canteen by, in my opinion, extreme people, tout my observation during fifteen years has been that the men who get intoxicated do so outside the camp. I am one of those who do not believe in these drastic means of protection for men or women ; I do not believe in legislating to have saints on earth. The wise way to govern men and women and to make them good, is to treat them as such. I have no doubt that friends of mine will strongly oppose what I am now saying, but I am conscientious in my opinion about it, and when I do believe that it is best for the men and for temperance in the end that the principle mentioned by the adjutant general be carried out, I am bound to stand up and defend my belief. If you do make a regulation and the responsible officers do not carry it out, then discharge the officers. There are a class of men who rebel against being compelled not to take what they think they have a right to take, and that particularly applies to beer. If you give these men soft drinks and beer they will stay in camp. I believe the adjutant general was wise in putting in his report this recommendation, and from my experience of fifteen years in camp, I believe it is right, and I am ready to defend it. The true temperance idea is not to go beyond what is reasonable and to take in moderation what a man believes he has a right to take. I am perfectly content that other people should not take liquor if they wish not to, but I say again that my experience is that the camps are in better order if you allow soft drinks and beer in the canteens. I believe that if it is an evil to have a cainteen, it is the lesser evil.

I wish to support the attitude of the Minister of Militia (Hon. Mr. Borden) in regard to the canteen. The hon. gentleman from South Norfolk (Hon. Mr. Tisdale)

has referred to the adjutant general as being favourable to the canteen. The adjutant general probably knows all about canteens, and he may know all about drill, but as the representative of a section of the Canadian people, I think I know more about the Canadian people and the sentiment of the Canadian people than he does. 1 take the responsibility of voicing what 1 believe to be that sentiment in this House, and it is in accordance with the position taken by the Minister of Militia.

I had no intention of offering any remarks in reference to the militia estimates, but I am inspired by the eloquent language of the hon. gentleman from Colchester (Mr. Gourley) to say a word or two. I disagree altogether from what my hon. friend from Winnipeg (Mr. Puttee) has said in connection with military matters. I am an old man now, but I remember when I was a captain in the militia of Prince Edward Island before confederation, when the Fenians were threatening to invade the shores of Canada, and got into certain parts of western Canada, but when they found that the people of Prince Edward Island were ready to up and fight them, they hurried back across the line.
Hear, hear.

As British freemen we should endeavour by all means possible to instruct our children from the moment they are able to receive instruction to be able to protect their country. The Minister of Militia has shown great patience in connection with this matter, and I hope there will be no discussion of these estimates, because if there is any hon. gentleman on the floor of this House who deserves the gratitude and thanks of the people of Canada, it Is that hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Borden). We know that not only has he used his best exertions to prepare the contingents for South Africa, but that his own son went to the front in defence of his country and shed his rich young Canadian blood on the yellow veldts of South Africa. It is therefore, I say, that we should offer no obstruction to the estimates brought down by the hon. minister, and that we should do all in our power to have them passed without criticism.
Oh, no, not at all.

Only in this respect, of course. The estimates should be subject to the criticism that the money should be expended properly, and that such estimates should only be brought down as are required in the interests of the people of Canada. Then they should pass without undue criticism. I want to say one word in regard to the first contingent. When the tocsin of war was sounded and British subjects were driven from their homes in South Africa to seek refuge in the cities and towns of the
coast; when we were threatened-because when British subjects in South Africa had to leave their homes, you can never tell when we in Canada may be threatened with a like calamity-our young men rallied to the front. They were prepared to go and shed their blood dn defence of the hearths and homes of the empire. Prince Edward Island was called on to supply a certain number of young men, and we sent a full quota of that contingent. These men rallied round the flag when the occasion required. They were ready, and more than ready to go forward and fight in the defence of thedr country, and hundreds more would have been ready if they had been required. My hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Hon. Sir Louis Davies) is not in his seat. He has not a word to say with regard to this first contingent. The men who first volunteered to go and fight in South Africa are entitled to receive the same pay at least as those who went afterwards ; but we find that they received smaller pay than the other two contingents. Those who remember the battle of Paarde-berg, when the wily Cronje was driven to the last ditch, will remember that when the morning dawned two young men from Prince Edward Island lost their lives in front of the enemy. The names of those two young men, Riggs and Taylor, will be for ever enshrined in the history of Prince Edward Island and dn the history of Canada. They went to the front and were found in advance of the trenches. It was rash perhaps, but they were impetuous and determined that the Boers should be conquered that morning. Those two noble young men shed their life's blood in defence of the empire, and their names will be held in remembrance by Canada for many years to come. Their comrades were equally ready to surrender their lives if necessary; and therefore, having fought the battles of the empire and having returned from the battlefields of South Africa, I think it is unjust and unfair that they should not receive the same compensation as those who followed. I trust that the hon. Minister of Militia will see, as a matter of justice, that the men of the first contingent receive equal pay with those of the second and third contingents.

The speech of the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat has brought to my mind a statement which I wished to make to the minister, and it is my apology for troubling the committee with a word or two more. I shall most heartily endorse the action of the minister if he can see his way to bringing in an additional item for making, according to the arm of the service, the pay of the first contingent equal to that of the second and the third. I was not aware before that there was any difference except what might be caused by the distinction between the dif-

ferent arms of the service. I am not1 prepared to vote an increase for one arm of the service without doing the same for all. There are military reasons why infantry, cavalry and artillery get different rates of pay. It is not necessary to go into those reasons, because they are recognized in all the armies in the world. For instance, a cavalryman has a great deal more work to do than an infantryman, because he has to take care of his horse. In my younger days, when I was a horseman and was sometimes too far away to get any one to take care of my horse, I never went to bed until I saw that the horse was properly attended to. No man deserves to have a horse who will not take care of it. But recognizing the distinction between the different arms of the service, I agree with the hon. member for West Prince (Mr. Hackett) that those who went first should, if possible, be even better recompensed than those who went later, though all were animated by the same spirit. So that if the minister can see his way to making an increase of that sort, I shall be most happy to support it.

The hon. gentleman who has just sat down is astray on this matter of pay. I do not think there is any distinction made in the rate of pay between cavalry and infantry. An infantryman and a cavalryman in the militia get the same rate of pay-50 cents a day. The allowance for a horse is one dollar a day ;( but that is for the horse not the man. So the argument of my ihon. friend falls to the ground. I cannot speak with authority with respect to the artillery, but I think the same thing is true of them. Therefore if that argument is used against the first contingent getting the same pay as the second and third, it is perfectly baseless. I think the first contingent should be placed in the same position as' the second and third. Surely this country is able to do justice by these men. Even if a contract was made, we are not necessarily to be bound by it in our treatment of the men. We should look at the matter from the standpoint of equity, and on that ground it seems to me the men of the first contingent are deserving of the same consideration that is given to the men. of the second and third.

speechtext:
Before the hon. minister goes, I would like to call his attention to something that, I think, ought to receive consideration at the hands of the government. It is with reference to the remounts that are being bought in Canada for the Imperial army. The hon. minister may 'say that he has no control over the matter : but, I am sure that representation made from his department and the Department of Agriculture to Major Dent would result in having the purchase made

on lines that would be more beneficial to the farmers of Canada than those now followed. My information is, that Major Deni, while in Canada, purchasing horses, to-day is buying through a single agent in Montreal and another in Toronto, who get a substantial sum for every horse that passes the examination there. Buyers who go out amongst the farmers to pick up these horses say it would be much better if an advertisement were sent out, and in each town a day was set when Major Dent and his assistant could 'select and purchase horses. Or, if this was thought not desirable, a time could be set when buyers could purchase them in the country and sell direct to Major Dent in Toronto, instead of to Walter Har-land 'Smith, who receives a substantial sum for each of them. Now, the information I have is this-Mr. Walter Harland Smith sends out buyers and says : I will 'allow you for every horse that passes the examination, $105. These horses will cost the War Department, probably, $145 or $150 on the average. The result is, that the purchaser who picks them up all over the country is obliged to buy at a figure which will enable him to sell at $105 each and pay for the culls left on his hands. It would be better to divide the profits between the buyer who picks the horses up and the farmer who sells them, instead of giving a middleman, without reason, this large amount, taken out of the buyer and the farmer. I thought that representations from the government would prevent that being done. I was talking to one of the buyers yesterday, and he told me that they were obliged to pay smaller prices to the farmers for the horses than they would be able to pay but for this arrangement.

The hon. gentleman has rightly supposed that I would say that we were in no way responsible. I may add that the Minister of Agriculture and myself were both quite ready to advise and assist the Imperial officers who came here, in any way in our power. Our services were offered in that behalf, particularly by the Minister of Agriculture. I do not know how far they were accepted, but I do know that Col. Dent is absolutely responsible for what is being done, and that he has had all the assistance he was willing to accept from the Department of Agriculture and from my own department. The British government sent him here, and sent assistants with him. They are paying all the bills. We have absolutely nothing more to do with it than we have to do with paying the hills for the war in South Africa. The British government are very much inclined to do their business in their own way, and we are not at all responsible. I regret if the result has been that the farmers, the owners of horses, are not getting what they ought to receive, or if some intermediate party is
getting more than he ought to. This discussion may have the effect of bringing especially this matter to the attention of Col. Dent, and I will say to the hon. gentleman that 1 shall be happy to see that a copy of the ' Hansard ' containing what has been stated here is sent to him as soon as it is printed.
speakername: The MINISTER OP MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: I am glad the hon. minister has intimated his willingness to do that. 1 am still of the opinion that if representations were made to the War Office of the Imperial government, setting forth the unfairness of the system by which the horses are bought, they would give instructions by which that trouble might he avoided.

That might be done. In addition to what I have already said, I will promise that a copy of this debate shall be sent to Lord Strathcona, our High Commissioner. I may say that Lord Strathcona has interested himself a great deal in this matter, and has induced the British government to buy horses in Canada. It is largely owing to the representations made by this government through Lord Strathcona that Col. Dent has come here now.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

North-west Mounted Police-Pay of force, $182,500.

The committee will see that there is an increase of $46,000 in these estimates over those of last year. The appropriation which was voted by parliament last year was $353,750, but I am sorry to say that we could not keep the expenditure within that figure, and we shall have to ask at a later stage a further appropriation of $60,000 ; that is to say, we find it is not possible to maintain the force for less than $400,000. This is the estimate for a force of 500 men and over 400 horses. When I took charge of the department in 1806. the expenditure in that year was $504,072.29. We thought that we could increase the number of the force and bring the expenditure down to about $300,000. But the following year the expenditure was $369,628; iu 1898-9 it rose to $402,628; in 1S99-1900 the expenditure was $351,583. Last year we took an appropriation for $353,750, but we found that it is not possible to maintain the force on that appropriation, that is to say, a force of 500 men and 400 horses. We find that the expenditure will range about $800 per man. We thought at one time it would be possible gradually to decrease the force, and that as the country was settled a less number of men would be

required. But iustead of decreasing the force we are compelled to distribute it oyer a larger area. At present we have nine principal depots:	At Itegina, Calgary,
Macleod, Prince Albert, Lethbridge, and so on; and we have about seventy different stations or places where we have certain members of the police force. In most of these small stations we have from one to three men, in some as many as five. At the principal depots, at Calgary, Macleod, Prince Albert and Lethbridge we have a number ranging from twenty upwards. The duties of these men are not only those of ordinary policemen, but they have to discharge other services to the settlers. For instance, as is well known by the hon. members from the North-west Territories, the police force are called upon to perform the very important duty of putting out prairie fires. That country is very liable to fires, and it is the duty of the men in the summer time to protect the settlers from prairie fires. Settlement is now proceeding north of the Saskatchewan and towards the Athabasca river and the Peace river, where there is a wooded country, and the services of the police are of the nature of bushrangers throughout that territory. Policemen are also called upon to put in force the Act against the admission of diseased cattle. These various duties compel the men to travel a good deal from place to place, and necessarily increase the expenditure. There is no increase in the pay of the men, which remains the same as it was before; but there is an increase in the different items. In subsistence, forage, fuel and light, there is an increase of $17,873; in clothing, repairs, renewals, horses, arms and ammunition, there is an increase of $20,873; in scouts, guides, billeting, transport of men and expenses of that character, there is a small increase of $2,500; then, new buildings and repairs, $5,000, making a total increase in the estimates over last year of $46,250. There is no increase in the number of men.

No, I do not think he was the senior officer. Mr. Mc-Illree was the senior officer.

Yes.

It is mainly for subsistence. In the items of fuel and light,
there is very little increase. The fuel that we use is chiefly wood and coal, and it is all supplied by tender.
The principal amount is for subsistence ?

Yes. The light is not supplied by tender. In most of the places where we have depots such as Cal-garv, Regina, Macleod, Prince Albert and other places, the light is supplied by electricity. Where we have small stations there is no charge for light, because the men are chiefly boarded, and the light is supplied.

No, we have another item for them. We have 250 men in the Yukon.

" No, there are two 7-pounders, four 9-pounders, and two mortars.
This is a pretty large increase from last year to be accounted for by the upward tendency of values in one year. Has the force been increased since last year ?

No, the force has not been increased, but last year we took an appropriation of $353,750. I have stated to the committee already that we could not keep the expenditure within that figure, and I will have to ask for a supplementary vote of $60,000. To maintain 500 men and 400 horses we cannot do with less than about $800 per man. I hope we will be able to reduce it in future years, perhaps this year, but the committee will readily understand that in the last few years the force has been somewhat demoralized by the changes which have taken place in order to send men to the Yukon and to take men back and send them to South Africa. We have had to bring in a number of new recruits, and the displacement alone has cost a great deal of money. That is the reason why I think the expenditure has been larger than it was estimated for. I believe that with normal conditions we would be able to reduce the cost of a man to a less figure than $800.
Has the force been kept up to its usual strength ?
There were 700 men when we took office. We have reduced the number to 500.
You have 250 additional men in the Yukon ?
Yes.
And 500 in the North-west Territories ?
Yes.
That makes 750 men altogether ?
Yes.
So that instead of the force being reduced it has been increased by 50 men ?

No, my hon. friend will remember that the Yukon was not in existence at that time. We take one appropriation for the force in the Northwest Territories, and for the force in the Yukon we take another appropriation.
Yes, but they are all mounted police ?	*
Yes, all mounted police.
I would like to ask the right hon. minister if he could give the figures for medical stores and stationery separately ?

I could not give my hon. friend these figures separately at this moment. The figures for stationery and medical stores are between $3,000 and $4,-
000.
But you could not say how they are divided ?
No.
What is the maximum price that the government allows to be paid for horses for remounts ?
One hundred dollars.
Upon whose recommendation was the force reduced ?
Upon the recommendation of the minister.

I have had some experience in the North-west Territories, and I think if there is one thing which would not be justifiable it would be the reduction of the police force which is one of the most competent bodies of the kind that I know of. I have had some experience in stockraising, I lived for a time in the North-west Territories, and I may say that if there is a body of men in the world that ought to be respected and honoured, it is this police force. I speak as an eastern man, and I say that instead of a reduction I would urge an increase in the force, because settlers all over the country are complaining of the reduction that took place. In reference to the statement of the right hon. gentleman in regard to fire guards, I may say that the little ranch that I was on was saved by these men who came at an extraordinary rate of speed when notice was given. They are the most extraordinary men in the world. The fire was sighted at what I thought several miles from our place, but it came bounding on and within an hour was quite near, but these men went to work with the appliances they have for fighting fires and they saved the properties of the neighbouring ranchers. If any body of people in this country deserve support I believe it is this body. To reduce their number would be to cripple their usefulness. The settlers that I heard from in all parts of the country complained of the reduction of the force that had been made.

My hon. friend {Mr. Gourley) lias paid a very just tribute to the police force. It is acknowledged to be one of the most efficient bodies of the kind in the world. It is not proposed to reduce the number of men, but I think that by careful administration we can reduce the cost of the maintenance of the men. We estimate it now at $800 per man. That is the estimate on which this appropriation that we are now asking is based. The force is coming back to normal conditions again, the Yukon is becoming settled more and more and perhaps we will be able to decrease the number of the force in the Yukon. As to the North-west Territories, I do not see that for some years to come we can very well reduce the number of the men. No doubt as the country develops the settlers wil be able themselves to perform the services which are now rendered by the police. But while that is true of the older part of the Territories, the settlement is advancing north of the Saskatchewan, and as we take mounted police from the settled parts we will probably have to send them amongst the new settlers. For some years I do not see that we can very well reduce the number of men.
New buildings and repairs, $15,000.

The increase of $5,000 is due to the fact that we have to renew the foundations of our buildings, which are some twenty years old now, at Calgary and Regina and other places.
Mounted Police, Yukon territory, $450,000.

While there was a large increase in the other item, there is a large decrease here. That is due to the fact that the facilities for communication in the Yukon are better, living is cheaper and consequently we think that we can supply 250 men for $450,000 instead of $500,000 as last year.
Is that for the erection of new buildings or for the rent of buildings ?
It is for new buildings.

I might remind the House that the North-west Mounted' Police force was originally organized by Sir A. A. Dorion, who was Minister of Justice in the Mackenzie government, and afterwards Chief Justice of Quebec. The regulations prepared for the force at that time are those which exist at the present day.
Compensation to members of the North-west Mounted Police for injuries received in the discharge of duties, $2,500.
I may read the following schedule of those who are now receiving compensation under this vote :
Duggan, J. P., synovitis, 23 rents per day. Guernsey, Charles, rheumatism, 23 cents per day
Canada Gazette, $7,000.
The increase of $1,000 here is owing to the increased price of paper and the advance in wages.
Is that due to the paper combine ?
I would not like to answer that too definitely.
I thought we were told this afternoon by the Hon. Mr. Sutherland that paper has become cheaper.

That is, cheaper than in former days.
Miscellaneous printing, $40,000.
The Secretary of State, under whose department this is, gives me the same explanation, namely, that the increase is due to the increased price of paper and higher wages.
This is a very thin House to-night, and as it may be that these items have be.en left over for discussion, perhaps some hon. gentlemen who are not present would like to discuss them.
I have no objection to allowing any of these items to stand.
I want to know why these items were left over.
These items have not been presented to the House before.
When did this increase of wages commence ?
I cannot give the time.

$30,000 was the original amount and the vote is increased by $9,200 or over 30 per cent in one year. It does not seem to me that the average increase of wages throughout the country would account for this.
Nor wages alone, but paper and wages.

Well, even paper and wages. I do not know that paper is so very much dearer than it was. We are getting more paper mills and pulp is being turned out in immense quantities. Have there been any more men employed ?

If my hon. friend desires it, I shall be very glad to get the information in detail. All the information that has been furnished to me is that this increase is due to an increase of about 25 per cent in paper and wages. I do not think there is any fixed standard for the number of persons employed in that department.

I understand that the government has not been getting all the printing done in the Printing Bureau, hut has been letting it out to friendly printing associations and newspaper offices at increased prices. Probably this accounts for the increase ?
I am sure there is no printing done outside that can be done in the Printing Bureau. It is only when the Printing Bureau is overcrowded that anything is done outside.
That is not giving the slightest information with regard to this item. Did that account for the increase, or was all this increase in the work of the Printing Bureau ?

That is my advice in the memorandum furnished me.
Expenses in connection with the Canada Temperance Act, $1,000.
What is the meaning of the increase ?

$500 is only sufficient to hold one election, and there is reason for believing there will be two.
Salaries and contingencies of the office of the Paris agency, $3,500.
This is the same vote as usual.

This item is in connection with Mr. Fabre's office. The right hon. First Minister will remember that there was considerable discussion on that matter, and some questions were asked as to whether Mr. Fabre would maintain the present outfit in Paris or not. He has a large suite of rooms there which I understand are wholly unnecessary to be maintained in
connection with his position. I believe Mr. Fabre has done very valuable service, and I would not be opposed to keeping up his office as it has been kept up in the past; but there has been a good deal of broadening out there. Perhaps the government are able to state whether the present scale of expense is to be maintained.

I am sorry to say I cannot give my hon. friend all the explanations he would like to have; but the present item is the same as we have voted for the last fifteen or eighteen years, and therefore it implies no new departure. If I might give my candid opinion, I would say that the appropriation is altogether insufficient. The quarters in which Mr. Fabre has maintained the office, all those who have been in Paris must acknowledge to be quite insufficient and quite unworthy of the position of Canada. It is in a good location in the centre of Paris, but in that locality Mr. Fabre could only obtain for the rent he could pay a very inferior office indeed. Last year while the exhibition was going on Mr. Fabre was allowed to have a larger office, and I think all the Canadians who were in Paris agree that the departure was a wise one, so far as the exhibition was concerned. If I had the management of the office, I would not hesitate to ask for a larger appropriation, so that Mr. Fabre could have better quarters. If hon. gentlemen will look at the paper published by Mr. Fabre, called Paris-Canada, they will find in each issue the numbers of Canadians who visit the office from week to week, and they will find that they are very large. Mr. Fabre is able to give valuable information to all visitors. If the minister in charge were to ask for a larger appropriation so as to afford Mr. Fabre's offices larger and better and more worthy of Canada than he has to-day, I believe my hon. friend would be the very first to vote the appropriation.

I have not been finding fault on the grounds the right hon. gentleman has indicated. I have not found any fault with Mr. Fabre, because I believe he has done good service with his paper. If it is necessary to provide a better office for Mr. Fabre than he had before, I do not think any one would complain; but the question was asked what was the intention of the government -with regard to retaining the rooms which were obtained to serve the purposes of the Paris exposition.
I have a very distinct recollection that when hon. gentlemen opposite were on this side of the House, they criticised this item year after year very freely, and condemned it most unmercifully.
Not I.

I will admit that the hon. gentleman did not, but some of his friends

did. The question was asked, what did Mr. Fabre do for this money ? He was supposed to be acting as an immigration agent ; but one year he managed to bring out one immigrant, another year I think he brought out three, and in other years he brought none at all. And I think a good many years none at all. During the Paris exhibition, more commodious rooms were selected aud furnished and perhaps properly so for the occasion, but is. it necessary to keep these up and for no useful purpose ? It may be that Mr. Fabre does work in other lines, but, so far as information is given to the House, he does not seem to do much work for Canada beyond remaining there as a representative of Canada. A few Canadians may call on him but we would like to have some work done for the expenditure.

I think this item might stand until the Agricultural Committee have heard Mr. Pedley, the head of the Immigration Department, who is to appear before the committee. He is immigrant agent over there, and we do not want to spend quite so much money for very little work. I do not believe that Mr. Fabre has sent us many immigrants.

I have no objection to let the item stand if the hon. gentleman desires. In answer to my hon. friend from Grey (Mr. Sproule) I recollect when this item was before the House in former years it was pretty well criticised, but I must pay him the compliment of never having joined in any of the criticisms on it, and I did not expect that he would depart from that very wise course to-day. With regard to the remarks of my hon. friend from Lennox (Mr. Wilson), 'I must say that Mr. Fabre is not doing very much in the way of sending immigrants from France to Canada.
What is his business proper ?

I will have to refer my hon. friend to the appointment of Mr. Fabre by his own friends as immigration agent twenty years ago. He never did very much as such, and I doubt if any one we sent to Paris would ever do much hi that way. The French peasantry would be a most valuable class of immigrants. We do not want any other kind of immigration from Europe but farmers, and the French peasant would be very valuable, because he is thrifty, sober and frugal and has all the good qualities. But he is very much attached to the soil of his own country and does not care to immigrate. Mr. Fabre, however, finding that he could not do much as immigration agent, turned his activity into other lines. He has been a very valuable agent of Canada all over Europe. He edits a paper, he is a literary gentleman of eminent culture, and has performed the duties of agent for the Canadian people and government. His office is open to all Canadians and very) Mr. SPROULK
well patronized. There Is not a Canadian who visits France but goes to the office of Mr. Fabre and gets there valuable information. My hon. friend will agree with me that although Mr. Fabre may not do much in the way of sending immigrants to Canada, we have reached such a stage of development that we can afford to maintain an agency in the second city of Europe next to London, where Canada and its affairs may be appreciated and made known to the people of France.
Why call him an immigration agent ?

My hon. friend has stated an objection to which I agree. I would rather call him the commissiary of the Canadian government.
Mr. LaRIVIERE. That is what he is called in Paris.

I would give him the title and the emoluments of a commissiary and perhaps might count on the support of my hon. friend.
Item allowed to stand.
Academy of Arts, $2,000.

This is not a grant to any particular building, but to the Royal Academy established a few years ago for the cultivation of fine arts in Canada, organized by Mr. O'Brien and other eminent artists. This organization holds exhibitions from place to place. It is to have an exhibition in Toronto shortly.
Cost of arbitration respecting the accounts between the Dominion of Canada and the provinces of Ontario and Quebec (payments on account of services rendered may be made to members of the Civil Service, notwithstanding anything in the Civil service Act), $3,000.
This is something we ought to have an explanation of.

A few years ago the grants for this service were very much larger, because the business before the arbitrators was more extensive. The arbitration has now been reduced to a very small scope, as we have disposed of all the disputed matters except that known as treaty No. 3. Recently we were approaching a conclusion of that matter, but were asked to suspend proceedings in order that the government of Ontario might make a proposal for a change in the arrangements. That proposal was made a short time ago, but we have not yet been able to comply with it. The Act provides that the arbitrators may deal with the matters referred to them, not in a strictly legal spirit, hut in the broader spirit of equity, and make such awards as might seem just. But if the arbitrators come to any decision upon a question of law, they are obliged to state that in their; award, and in that case there is the right to appeal. There is no

appeal on ordinary questions of fact, but only on points of law. The government of Ontario desired to broaden the scope of the appeal, and proposed that we should introduce legislation to that effect. As there were three parties to the arbitration, Ontario, Quebec and the Dominion, we thought we should first ascertain whether the province of Quebec would join in this application. That province, however, dissented from the application, and the matter did not go further. At an early day the arbitrators will meet, and the whole business will close up.
Classification of old records of Canada In the office of the Privy Council (payments on account of this service may be made, notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act), $1,000.
To assist in defraying the cost of the publication of documents Issued by the Canadian Mining Institute, $1,000.
Is this service proceeding from year to year ?
It has been going on some twenty years or so. The work is accumulating every year, and I am afraid we will never see the end of it.

I hope the hon. gentleman is not allowing it to get ahead of him.
Miscellaneous-Contribution towards publication of International Catalogue of Scientific Literaturo, $500.
That seems to he new. What is it ?

My hon. friend, the Secretary of State, has furnished me with a memorandum which shows that at the instance of the Royal Society of England, Lord Strathcona has arranged that Canada should join other nations in publishing the International Catalogue of Scientific Literature. The United Kingdom has agreed to take forty-five sets, Germany sixty-five, France thirty-five, and other nations in proportion. The Cape of Good Hope will take five sets, and Canada has promised to take five sets.
That is $100 a set ?

Yes. it is an expensive work.
Some resolutions reported.

It is our intention on Monday to take up the Election Bill, and then go on with supply, taking up the estimates of the Minister of Public Works, or of the Minister of Railways, if he is able to be here.

speakername: The SOLICITOR GENERAL (Hon. Chas. Fitzpatrick) moved :

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I beg to say that I have the Governor General's assent to this resolution, as well as to the following one.

That it is expedient to amend the Act respecting the judges of provincial courts and to provide as follows :-
1.	That the salary of the chief justice of the Supreme Court of the North-west Territories shall be $5,000, and of the four puisnS judges of the said court each $4,000 per annum.
2.	That the salary of an additional judge of the Territorial Court of the Yukon territory shall be $5,000 per annum.
3.	That the salaries of the seventeen puisne judges of the Superior Court of Quebec, whose residences are fixed at Montreal or Quebec (including the judge to whom the district of Terrebonne is assigned), shall be each $5,000 per annum.
speakername: The SOLICITOR GENERAL (Hon. Chas. Fitzpatrick) moved :

speechtext: Motion agreed to.

House in Committee of Supply.
Harbours and rivers, Prince Edward Island, $42,500.
['We shall probably take up the Election Bill in the afternoon, if found convenient. Following that, we shall proceed with the estimates of the Minister of Railways.']
I would like to ask the minister a question which, strictly speaking, should have been asked in connection with the Nova Scotia items ; that is, the cost of the shed and the wharf at Salmon River.
That shed has cost about $300.
speakername: The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS (Hon. J. I. Tarte).

speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman at some future time ask his deputy to let me know precisely the. cost of that work at Salmon River ?
With pleasure.

Is the minister prepared to make any provision for the protection and preservation of the wharfs at Pictou Island ? I have received information that they require some attention this year in order to prevent their destruction.

I will look carefully into the question. My attention has been called to it by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Bell, Pictou), and by other gentlemen also. When the supplementary estimates come, I will be in a position to give a more definite answer.
Cascumpec Harbour-Closing opening through beach, $2,000.
What amount of money was expended for this same purpose last year? Was it let by contract or days' work, and is it the intention of the minister to carry it out by day's work this year ?
The total estimated cost is $3,500. Last year $1,500 was spent, and $2,000 is asked this year to complete the work.

Some years ago a large amount of money was expended for blasting rock at the entrance of Cascumpec harbour, and it was believed that by the blasting of this rock the outflow of water from the harbour would not be impeded. Is it the intention of the minister to continue the work of blasting the rock there, which was found to be very beneficial. If that work had been continued this opening would not have been made through the sand-hills at all.
I have no information as to the blasting of that rock. I will take a note of what the hon. gentleman says, and I will ask Mr. Egan to inquire into it.
What is the nature of that work ?
We have a resident engineer who has been employed for twelve or fifteen years, and it is on his report that we carrv out the work. This is to close a gap in the beach.

I believe that money should be expended on this work, and so far the appropriation is perfectly correct. Last year $1,400 was expended, and it was simply thrown away there by day's labour. There was no competition In connection with the work. There should have been a contract. The early freshets of the spring carried the work that was done out to sea. There was no permanent work done there.
I approve of the expenditure of this money, but the minister should see that it is not placed in the hands of political friends and favourites. The work should be put up to
109*
competition, and the money expended properly and in the interests of the people.

The work has been successfully carried out, and I will carry it on in the same way as formerly.
Public Works-Hurd's Point-Repairs to pier, $350.
I should like to know what this amount is to be used for.

It is called for by Mr. Egan, the resident engineer, and the acting .chief engineer, for the completion of repairs.
Miminegash breakwater, &c., $1,500.
What is this money intended for ?
This is required by Mr. Egan and the acting chief engineer for levelling and close piling the ends and sides of the breakwater, replacing a portion, and effecting some general repairs.

Yes, I remember that a year or two ago a contract was let for the extension of the Miminegash breakwater, and when the contract was completed the outer end of the breakwater was found to be about two feet under water, and it is necessary now to raise and bring it up to the proper level. The expenditure of this money is very necessary. Miminegash is an important harbour of refuge on the west side of Prince Edward Island, and it is necessary to have money spent there to improve the harbour. The work for which this money is asked should have been carried out last year. The sum of $1,200 was expended last year, and the minister will remember very well how it was expended- in building a brush fence over the sand hills for the purpose of giving employment to his followers previous to the election ; and when the first storm of the fall came, nearlv the whole of that brush fence was carried away. If the minister is going to do some close piling and raise the end of the pier, there would be no difficulty in making a plan of the work ; and I trust that he will not place it in the hands of his followers, but put it up to tender so that all classes will have an opportunity of competing for the work.

This is a small sum which is asked to complete the work. The whole community will benefit by that work. My hon. friend asks me to put it up to tender. The House will not share his view. I do not object to ask for tenders for large works, but small works such as this cannot be successfully done by contract. We would spend more money in publishing advertisements for tenders than we would in carrving out tbii work.

This is not for repairs ; it is to complete a new work. The hon. gentleman knows wrhat that new' work is and what is required to be done, and I am sure the people would willingly pay the cost of advertising in order to have it put up to competition, so that all contractors m Canada will have an opportunity of competing for it, instead of the money being paid to a few favourites of the government.
* Mr. CLANCY. My bon. friend from Prince (Mr. Hackett) has made the statement that the money expended last year on this work w-as frittered away among favourites of the government. This is a small sum, and I do not imagine that the committee is at all inclined to criticise the expenditure if it is necessary ; but the minister has made no reply to that statement. We have come to a time when I think the committee may well demand of the 'lion, gentleman that he draw the line somewhere between contract work and day's labour.

I certainly do not intend to ask for tenders in this case. Last year we spent $1,819.1(5 In effecting repairs on the northern breakwater and constructing protection works. This vote is practically for a continuation of the work, and I intend to carry it out by day's labour, because I feel, as I have long felt, that w'orks of small importance are better and more economically done by day s labour than by contract. You buy your own material, and you pay the men just w'hat the contractor pays them. The work last year was successfully carried out. I may say that I have kept the same old Conservative engineer who was there when I took office.
Why did you not dismiss him ?

I am scarified more than if I had done so. and had appointed a Liberal. I have kept him because he is doing the work well. I am sure that he does not exclude every Conservative on the island, and surely my hon. friend will not insist that I ask for tenders. The work is a very useful one, and I do not see why we should discuss it any more.

I think that the appropriation for Miminegash properly expended will be of great advantage, and I am finding no fault with the minister for the amount placed in the estimates. But when he speaks about the resident engineer being a Conservative, I know nothing about that, and can tell him that he has nothing to do with the employing of the men. He simply makes his plans and specifications, which are placed in the hands of a follower of the government, who sees that no Conservatives can get a day's work on those public works.
There is another work not mentioned in the estimates, but of great importance, required at a place about ten miles distant from Miminegash. It is a place called Skinner's Pond. Around the coast we have many of these ponds, separated from the gulf by a narrow belt of sand. They can be made of great utility to the fishermen, if proper works are done to utilize the waters in those ponds. The people of Skinner's Pond, who are mostly fishermen, desire to have some work done there. I asked a short time ago what amount had been expended, and was told that $1,462 had been spent there last year. 1 asked what engineer had reported and was told that Mr. Egan had reported on the 29th of September, 1898. I asked when the work had begun and was told on the 30th of September, 1900, exactly two years after the engineer had reported and one month and seven days before the elections. I asked the minister whether he had an appropriation for that work, and he said no, that the money had been paid out of special appropriations for the repairs of harbours and piers in Prince Edward Island. Forty men were put to work at Skinner's Pond, thirty-seven days before the elections, and were kept at work for some days afterwards. That work was done when it was required very much, not for the needs of the people, but for the purpose of electing a supporter of the government. Why did the hon. gentleman sleep two years over the matter ? When he had his report on the 29th of September, 189S, why did he wait until the 30th of September, 1900 1 He slept two years, but on the 29tli of September, 1900 he had a vision in which he was told that if he did not begin the work then, his candidate would be defeated and wiped out. He then expended $1,400, but I see nothing in the estimates to continue the work. It is a work of great magnitude. The hon. gentleman began by digging a channel through the sand bank between the pond and the gulf, and that work must be continued. There is no natural outlet there at all, and he should in the supple-mentaries provide $5,000 at least to complete the digging of this channel as well as erect a pier at the outer end, in order that the outflowing or inflowing waters may concentrate in the channel.

I cannot keep in mind all the reports from the resident engineers, but I am advised that to carry out that work would cost about $20,000. That is a large amount. My hon. friend is a most economical man in public matters generally, but when his own locality is concerned he wants to spend a large amount of money. I am a careful man and am prepared to spend the money when I get full information, but until then I stay my hand. I shall take advantage of all the information which my hon. friend offers, for I always receive his opinion with a great deal of consideration. Supposing we have spent some money there, that ex-

penditure has been useful. I deeply sympathize with the fishermen and will do everything I can to help them.

I want to give my hon. friend full credit for what he is doing in improving the harbours in the islands. He has done a great deal for us, but if this work is to cost $20,000, why does the hon. gentleman, just prior to the election, throw away $1,500 on it ?
We have done some work which is useful [DOT]and are not bound to spend everything asked for. Later on, if we find it is useful to spend more money, we will do so.
Useful for what ?

This is a pond, in which there was an opening into the sea not large enough to enable fishing boats to come in. Last year my hon. friend enlarged that channel, and that enlargement has been a great advantage as the hon. member admits. Before I left Prince Edward Island, I was waited on by a deputation of gentlemen from both sides of politics, who asked me to thank the Minister of Public Works for what he had done. They said it was a great boon as far as it went, but that a great deal more ought to be done and could be done by making a harbour there. I said that was a big business, involving a lot of money. I asked how much it would cost, and they could not tell exactly, and I promised that when I came to Ottawa, I would visit the Department of Public Works and look into the matter. I found that the report of the engineer showed that to carry out the new work required would cost $20,-
000.	I think that the Minister of Public Work did very well, as far as he went, and did a great deal better to stay his hand and give consideration to this very large expenditure. I did not feel my way clear to take grants from other parts of the island and spend $20,000 trying to make a harbour just at this place. My hon.'friend (Hon. Mr. Tarte) said he would consider the matter, and that is a fair answer to give.
New London-Repairs to breakwater, &c. $3,600.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Is that under contract or by day's labour ?

We have called for tenders. We spent $248 there last year.
Public Works-Chargeable to Income-Harbours and Rivers, P.E.I.-Rustico (south)-Repairs to pier, $1,500.
Is this to complete the work of repair ?

If my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Tarte) will permit me, I might explain that Rustico pier is one of the piers on the north
side of the island concerning which there has been more or less difficulty for many years back. Last year, I visited the place, and the neighbours gathered round and showed me what was required to be done there. The water rushing out of Rustico harbour goes through a circuitous channel, and the difficulty is, with the breakwater to keep the harbour from filling up. There are two channels in Rustico harbour. And the present idea, in which the local resident engineer concurs, is that there should be an ' L' built on the existing breakwater and stop the water to the westward and send the volume of water out through the main channel. It is for this work that the vote is asked. This is one of the largest fishing stations on the north side of Prince Edward Island.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Will $1,500 finish the work ?

Yes.
Public Works-Chargeable to Income-Harbours and Rivers, P.E.I.-Souris, Knight's Point -Strengthening breakwater, $5,000.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: What is this ?

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Hackett) knows the Souris breakwater. It has been there for twenty-five years. It forms a harbour of refuge not only for the colonial but for the American fishermen, and it is essential that it should be kept in thorough repair. To this end, it must be strengthened every year. As the hon. gentleman knows, last year one of the most devastating storms ever known in the maritime provinces struck our coast, and this pier received shaking and damage. I have seen as many as from fifty to sixty colonial and American fishing vessels lying under the shelter of the breakwater. It would be nothing less than a public crime for any Minister of Public Works to allow this work to go down or get out of repair. It is the most important breakwater, by long odds, in Prince Edward Island, and it must be retained in thorough repair, or the fishermen will have no harbour of refuge there at all.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: How much was spent there last year ?

The amount was $1,125.
. Mr. HUGHES (King's, P.E.I.) This vote is for rip-rapping the seaward side of the breakwater with hard stone from Nova Scotia. There is no hard stone found in the island. Last year, $13,000 was voted, and a contract was let. But it was late in the season and the contractor was unable to do the work. He will not be able to do very much of the work before the 30tli June this year, and that is the reason of this

vote. While X am on my feet, I would like to say that I think the hon. member for West Prince (Mr. Hackett) gave a wrong impression to the House when speaking a few moments ago with reference to Skinner's Pond, he said that the resident engineer reported in 1898 upon the necessity of that work and that it was not until last year that it was commenced. Now, the engineer reports on all the works or contemplated works on the island each year, hut, of course, all the works cannot be taken up in one year

they must take their turn, the more necessary works first, and the others later. Sometimes it is three or four years after a report is sent in before a work can be commenced. I think the hon. member for West Prince wished to give the impression that this work at Prog Pond was purposely kept back. I do not think this was correct-it is the ordinary state of affairs that it is some time after the report is made before the work can be commenced.

I hope the hon. gentleman (Mr. Hughes, King's, P.E.I.) does not question the accuracy of my statement.
Mr. HGUGHES (King's, P.E.I.) I do not question it ; at the same time, the impression conveyed to the House might be incorrect. If I were a stranger and knew nothing about the facts, I would suppose that the work had been purposely kept back till the eve of the election. Such was not the case, because some works must be kept back after the year in which the engineer reports upon them. Some are being held over this year.
I understand from the hon. gentleman (Mr. Hughes, King's, P.E.I.) that the contract was let just on the eve of the election. Perhaps the hon. Minister of Public Works could give us the exact date.

I think the contract was awarded late. The House sat until August, and we could not take up all the work at once. Besides, I was away; but when I came back. I hurried the work as much as I could, and my hon. friend (Hon. Sir Louis Davies) helped me.
In any case, the work was let by tender.
speakername: The MINISTER OP MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Yes, it was by tender. At- the same time, it was not long before the election.
Could the hon. gentleman give us the exact date ?
I think it was the 2nd of November.
Oh, oh.

Oh, we were quite sure to carry the electiou -it made no difference.
Mr. HUGHES (King's, P.E.I.)
At what time was the work commenced ?

The work was started immediately.
Mr. HUGHES (King's. P.E.I.) The work has not been commenced yet.

Yes, we have spent there $1,100.
Mr. HUGHES (King's, P.E.I.) That was for carpenter work.
We would like to get the minister and the hon. member (Mr. Hughes, King's, P.E.I.) into harmony if we could. One says the work was commenced immediately, the other says it has not been commenced yet.
What the hon. gentleman (Mr. Hughes, King's, P.E.I.) said was that the stonework had not been started, but the carpenter work-the repairs had been begun.
At what time ?
Immediately, I suppose.
The expenditure took place during the summer.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Instructions were given on the 9th of August to go on with the carpenter work. That was before the elections were even decided upon.
But at what date was this work commenced ?

Perhaps my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Tarte) would allow me to explain. The work for which this money has been voted has not been commenced. Tenders were called for and the contract let at the beginning of last November. It is to riprap the outside of the pier with Nova Scotia stone. That will be done this summer. There was carpenter work to be done in repairing the woodwork on the breakwater, and that was done, but not a dollar was spent on the rip-rap.
speakername: The MINISTER OP MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: This is getting into a most dreadful state of confusion. I understand less about it, the more the Minister of Marine and Fisheries explains it. There was a sum of $13,000 in the estimates last year. Now, either the whole or part or none of that was expended.
There was $1,100 out of that spent for carpenter work. The balance is for stonework which has not yet been carried out.

I think the hon. Minister of Public Works is quite right about it. Now, what we want to ascertain is wdien that work involving the expenditure

of $1,100 last year was commenced, and over what period the contract extended.

The acting chief engineer informs me that instructions were given in the month of August-as to the exact date when the work was started, I am not prepared to say. But, if the hon. gentleman (Mr. Borden, Halifax) desires it, I can get the date.

Perhaps the
hon. gentleman will give us the exact date later on.
With pleasure.

The date ,at
which the advertisements were sent out calling for tenders.
They were certainly sent out in the month of October, because the contract was awarded on the 2nd of November.
Did tlje advertisements specify the work which has been referred to by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries ?
I do not know.
That is very mysterious.

There is nothing mysterious about it. Tenders were called for repairs of the stone work on the outside of the pier, called during the summer, and the contract was awarded on the 2nd of November to the lowest tenderer. The carpenter work was done during the summer, but it had nothing to do with this.
speakername: Tbie MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: It had something to do with this pier, had it not 7
Yes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I want to ascertain whether the advertisement sent out included this work involving an expenditure of some $1,100.
No.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: It did not cover that part of the work. That was done by day's labour, and then tenders were asked for to cover the stone work.
At that time the department must have understood the exact position of the carpenter work.
The carpenter work that has been done, the chief engineer tells me, was simply repairs of the piers. There was no new work at all about it.
It was an ordinary expenditure of money for ordinary repairs.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: The whole of this work is repairs, is it not 7
Rip-rapping the outside pier with stone.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: My hon. friend perhaps is not quite conversant with that kind of work. Suppose there is a pier exposed to the big waves of the sea, that pier is formed of carpenter work, not only there but elsewhere. Now, we repair the cribwork that has been injured, but to strengthen the pier it has been found necessary by the engineers to riprap the work, in other words, to place about the cribwork big stones, just as we do elsewhere, as we are doing now at Cape Tormentine. That is the kind of work for which these tenders for stone have been called.

I understand what rip-rapping is, I have been over this work possibly a good many times, but I never could understand why a part of the work, such as this expenditure of $1,100 represents, was not included in the general tender.
That could not be, because it was simply a repair. That part of the work was all timber, cribwork, within which the stone had to be placed. Not the same thing at all.

No, it is not the same thing, but it is all on the same pier, and possibly a separate tender might have been invited. I cannot understand why it is that part is done by day's work and part by tender. I suppose there must have been some good reason for it.

If the hon. gentleman was Minister of Public Works-and for his own sake I do not wish him to be-he would know that repairs can always be better carried out by day's labour than by tender. When you begin to repair a work you never know how much is to be done.

I see last year a vote was taken for $13,000, of which $1,100 has been spent, and the hon. gentleman asks now for $5,000. Does he propose to abandon the work that was then in contemplation, or why does he now only ask for $5,000 7 That vote was taken on the eve of a general election, for $13,000.
Let me call the hon. gentleman's attention to the nature of the vote. We are asking for this $5,000 to rip-rap the work, we do not ask it for the same work for which we took a vote last year.
Is the gentleman who has the contract for the rip-rap work the same man who did the carpenter work ?
No.
What is the name of the man who did the carpenter work ?
I have not his name just now, hut I will give it to my hon. friend.
Is it not a fact that the money for this so-called carpenter work went to the late contractor as extras just before the election ?
I will give the name of the man who did the carpenter work. My officers have taken a note of it, there is no secret about it.
Was not the name John T. Brennan ?

I will give the name with pleasure.
Summerside Harbour-Breakwater, $15,000.

This appropriation for the Summerside breakwater has been in the estimates for the last four years, but there is no breakwater yet.
