The matter has been used during several elections for the purpose of getting votes ; but the needs of the people, the shippers at Summerside, have apparently been a secondary matter in the mind of the Minister of Public Works. On February 13, I asked a question of the minister, and found that a contract had been let to McDonald & Moffat for $55,900. The contract was let on May 25, 1900, and the work was to he commenced at once, and to be finished on the 25th of November, 1901. The reply was that nothing had been done. Now, we have nearly entered into another year since the contract was let, and I would like to know whether the contractors intend to go on with this contract. If they do not, and if the work is necessary, as the engineers have reported, I would like to know the reason of the delay. I trust that this important work will be pushed forward at once, as it is very essential to our winter communication, and I also hope the minister will favourably consider the building of a pier at Gordon's Point, about which I asked a question some days ago.

That Summerside work has created a good deal of attention in the department. Ready as we were to do the right thing by Summer-side, we were frightened by the vast amount of money that the plans called for. I visited the place myself a few years ago with the present acting chief engineer. If I remember right, the first plans would have entailed an expenditure of $125,000. We Mr. TARTE.
thought that was too large a sum of money to ask for, and we made new plans which while being sufficient will involve less money. Tenders were asked for, and the present contractors are Messrs. McDonald & Moffat, who took the contract for $55,900. They are now proceeding with the work.
I grant there has been a little delay, but I am glad to inform the hon. gentleman that the two contractors have set to work, and we expect the work will, be carried on speedily and to a successful conclusion.
Tignish-To complete repairs and extension of breakwater, $500.
What does this exten-si9n consist of ?

This vote of $500 is required to complete the construction of the addition to the outer block, 60 feet by 40 feet, at the outer end of the northern breakwater in Tignish harbour. The resident engineer is asking for that amount to do the work which I have just described.
West Point-Extension of pier, $2,000.
What depth of water will you have when this work is completed ?
I have not the information at hand, but my ! officers are taking a note of it and will give it to my hon. friend (Mr. Hackett) to-morrow morning.
Is that work being done under contract ?
Yes.

There is another work that I would like to call to the attention of the hon. minister, and that is at Brae, which is about ten miles from West Point. I do not see any appropriation in the estimates for the Brae work. That work has been going on for many years and to make it available you will have to continue it still further until you get beyond the sand bank on the'side of the channel. I trust the hon. minister will see his way to having an amount placed in the supplementary estimates to provide for the further prosecution of the work at Brae.
The* MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS. Our attention has been called to that work in the same way that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Hackett) now calls our attention to it. I cannot promise anything, but. I repeat that our attention has been called successively to that work.
Wood Island (south)-Extension of breakwater, $700.
The, MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS. Under contract and this is to complete the work.

New Brunswick-Back Bay-Towards extension of wharf, $4,900.
What is the nature of that work ?	,
Tenders have been asked, but the contract is not yet awarded. It will be awarded to the lowest tenderer, of course.
What has been done with the $800 appropriated last year ?
We did not spend any money last year, so my officers tell me.
What depth of water will you have at low water at the end of the pier ?

The present pier is 150 feet long and 20 feet wide. It Is proposed to lengthen it by 56 feet, and to add a block at the outer end which will reach a depth of eight feet at low water and thirty-two feet at high water.
Will this work be let by tender 1
Yes, tenders are asked for now.
The work is very credit able to the government, I must say.
Does this sum which is asked for complete the work ?

There will be $2,000 in the supplementary estimates. This will not cover the whole cost of the work. We are not sure what the amount of the tender will be and it may be necessary to have $2,000 additional.
Then, I understand the hon. gentleman to say that the sum he is going to ask for later in the supplementary estimates, is intended to cover the whole expenditure on that work '!

Quite so.
Bay du Vin-To complete extension of wharf, $2,750.

By contract.
Burnt Church-Wharf, $3,900.
The; MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS. By contract also.
Campobello (Wilson's Beach)-Repairs to breakwater, $6,000.
Has this work been let by tender ?

We asked for tenders and we did not get any. Public tenders were asked for in the newspapers in the usual way and we did
not receive any. Then, we made up our minds to proceed by day's labour.

The reason probably is that they were fooled down there about this matter. They did not assume for a moment that the government meant to do the work and men would not necessarily fool their time away with it. To allow work like this, which will run into thousands of dollars, in a location like Campobello, to be let by day's work is an outrage on the country. There is a great rise and fall of tide at this point. I believe the maximum of the tide is 28 or 30 feet, and to attempt to put green hands at work to build a pier of this character is a waste of public money. This is a desirable work, a work that should have been prosecuted by the late government, perhaps, to a greater extent than it was. But, this government have allowed three, four, or five years to elapse when they knew from their engineer's reports that it was necessary to make repairs to this work and these reports will show that their neglect to make these repairs will entail an expenditure of $2,000 or $3,000 additional. To-day we have the spectacle in that county of a work that will cost from $15,000 to $25,000, if it is completed as it should be, let by day's labour to men who know nothing whatever about wharf building.

I am always surprised when I hear a gentleman who is in business speaking about an outrage in a case like this. One would imagine that no important work in this country is carried on by day's labour. Look at the work that is going on in the port of Montreal where a $3,000,000 undertaking is being carried on in the most successful way by day's labour. This is not the only part of the country in which day's labour has been adopted.' Railway and other important companies carry on work by day's labour. In this case I do not feel that I am guilty of any outrage. I asked for tenders. Tenders were not received. Was it my duty to carry out the work for which parliament had voted money or not ? I was instructed to carry out this work, I have canned it out and the hon. gentleman is not pleased. I did not receive tenders, because, he says the people thought we were not serious. Well, that is a very poor excuse. The work has been successfully carried on under the direction of a very able man-Mr. Shewan. He is not always agreeable to hon. gentlemen opposite.' far from it. Here is another case in which I left in his position a man who had been appointed by our opponents. He lias the supervision of this work. They have been warned, they have been notified, and if they do not carry out their work as they should do they will suffer. I did not receive any tenders and so I gave it by day's work. My hon. friend (Mr.. Ganong) is very hard to please.
Was it Mr. She wan who looked after that work ? No ; it was a local heeler of the Liberal party, who was instructed to look after that.

Mr. Shewan has supervision of the whole work. Of course, I suppose the foreman was one of our political friends. My hon. friend (Mr. Ganong) is enough of a sound business man to admit that when he is in office he will not select his foremen from this side of the House if he can find good men on his side. There are plenty of good foremen on the other side of the House and he can get them. When my friends opposite are in office I will not cry if they employ their own friends. That is fair dealing.

My hon. friend (Mr. Ganong) characterized this in a very mild term when he said it was an outrage. Here is a work costing $25,000, and the object of the minister in giving it out by days' labour is clearly to take the public money to bribe people with it. He will give no chance to the workmen of this country who do not belong to his political stripe. If he gave the work by tender the contractors would employ men irrespective of politics.
I asked for tenders and received none, and what am I to do ?

You should do as any business man or any man of common sense would do ; you should, as custodian of the public money, ask for tenders again, and I venture to say that the minister could get them. The hon. gentleman says that he had instructions to do that work. Who did he get these instructions from ?
From this very parliament.

And the minister had instructions from parliament to carry on the work to which my friend from West Prince referred, but he did not do it until two years afterwards. It is time that the minister (Hon. Mr. Tarte) should cease putting up Conservatives, whether they are local engineers or not, as buffers, between him and his department. The hon. gentleman is too much in the habit of doing that.
No.

The Minister of Public Works tells us that this man is a Conservative and a good officer. If he is a man of sense, he knows that his head would fall in the basket in twenty-four hours if he interfered with the political friends of the minister controlling the work, or allowed any but political friends of the minister to work at it. I know of no greater public scandal in Canada to-day than that a minister of the Crown should corruptly-I am using a Mr. TARTE.
mild term when I say it-corruptly take the money of the people to do this by days' work, his only object being to help his political friends. I deny that a public work can be carried out in a clean and successful manner under such circumstances. The minister (Hon. Mr. Tarte) sets out the plea that there is a resident engineer who is a good Conservative and who has been troublesome to his party, but I venture to say that he is not troublesome to his party now. It is the duty of the minister, before he gets any more estimates, to give a pledge, which I presume he will keep, that all works of that magnitude should be let by tender and that he should cease presenting that old excuse which is now so unsavory as to be almost unpresentable longer, namely, that lie does this for the purpose of helping the workingman. There is no Conservative in this House who would pretend to say that the party in power has not the right to serve its own political friends, but, the Minister of Public Works has gone beyond that. He has taken the work away from public competition and he has given it out by days' labour in order to exclude every workingman who is not a Liberal. No minister of the Crown is justified in doing that. I admit frankly that there are cases where you cannot do a work by tender and contract, but a minister ought to be scrupulously careful in this, and if he errs at all, it should be on the side of tender and contract. It may be true, as the minister says, that works have been successfully carried out by days' labour, but if so, it is an accident. The principle is unsound. No great railway corporation will let work by days' labour Unless it is done under their own men. There is no safe way of guarding the public treasury except by the rule of contract and tender. It is a rule that is contended for with great energy and vigour and ability by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright) in days past. How does he feel to-day, sitting silently beside the Minister of Public Works, who goes on regardless of the principle of tender and contract, and who is dribbling out the public funds of this country under the pretense of giving work to the labouring men ?

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Clancy) is at times reasonable, but at other times party spirit makes him take the wrong side of things. I have never known a case which is more simple than this one. I asked for tenders, I did not get any tenders, I started the work. I was pressed to carry out the work, the materials are there and the work is started. Am I not to go on with it ? If I had wished to commit that abominable outrage over which the hon. gentleman grows eloquent, I would not have asked for tenders ; but I asked for tenders, and tenders did not come. I then proceeded to do the

work by day labour. I take exception, not in a party spirit, but in a general way, to the doctrine laid down by the hon. gentleman.

The hon. gentleman will pardon me. It was laid down by the hon. gentleman's own friends, and contended for by them for years and years, and I venture to say that if they were on this side ot the House, they would contend for it to-day.
I invite the hon. gentleman to allow me to settle my case with my friends.
You must settle it with mine too.

I am prepared to settle it with the hon. gentleman now ; but, he will let me settle my difficulties with this side of the House. No man of sound business experience will say that work cannot be successfully carried out by day labour. What does the contractor do, after all ? He gets a contract from my department or any other, and he engages day labour for the work. Why, then, should not the officers of a well-conducted department be able to carry out the work just as well as the foreman of the contractor ? I cannot understand the doctrine that is laid down here. It simply means that no minister can find good foremen or good officers. There is no sense in that. I feel as able to find good foremen as Mr. Davis or Mr. Onderdonk, or any other contractor in the world. I have no objection to asking for tenders when the public interest requires it. It gives me a great deal less trouble. When a contract is awarded, I appoint an inspector of tne works, and I am through with it-that is, when the contractor is a good man. But when the contractor is an incapable man, and a man who has no means, I am not sure at all. My experience since I have been in office has convinced me that the system of the lowest tenderer, as it is practised in this country is a dangerous one. If we did what is done in France, in England, and in Germany- asked for tenders from a list of selected ' competent men-I would go in every time for the lowest tender ; but, when an 'incompetent man, a man who has no means, and who does not know his business, gets a contract by public tender, he puts you in deep water more than you may suppose. Such contractors do not pay their men. they do not pay for what they buy, they do not go on promptly and rapidly with the work. Of course, there are good contractors, but there are also a lot of contractors who tender low because they expect that if they get the contract something will turn up. Coming back to this work, I say I have done my duty. My hon. friend is not right or fair when he speaks of outrages. I have never committed any outrages to my knowledge. As a minister, I may have made mistakes ; but I have tried to be fair. My hon. friend reproaches me by saying that I have kept in the different provinces officers who were appointed under the late administration. I do not try to shield myself behind them. I only mention them to prove that I have not acted unfairly. It would have been easy for me to cut off the heads of some of these officers, because they are only temporary employees ; but, I keep them because I believe that when I have a good servant it is my duty to keep him. I know that my view is not shared Dy all my political friends ; it is not shared by my hon. friends opposite either; but that is my personal view. I give my patronage to my political friends first; it is my duty to do that; but, so far as the heads of branches are concerned, I have kept those who have done their duty, even when they have not been appointed by order in council. I believe I have acted fairly, and I do not think I deserve the reproaches too often levelled against me on that account. I would rather, perhaps, deserve reproaches from this side of the House. If I acted improperly in mentioning names, I will not mention them again. I am responsible for everything I do.
I am somewhat surprised at the criticism of the hon. member for Charlotte (Mr. Ganong) with regard to this work.
No one is opposed to the work.

No, but when the minister states that he advertised for Iiublic tenders and did not receive any, the hon. gentleman knows that he did what every good business man would have done -put in charge of the work an officer of the department in whom he had confidence, and left him to carry it out. I agree with the minister, that on general principles it is better in all possible cases to advertise for public tenders; but, everybody with any experience of business knows that when men without experience and without capital get contracts because their tenders are the lowest, the work is generally delayed, is poorly done and very unsatisfactorily done, and in the end costs the country a great deal more money. We have had instances of that at different times in previous sessions. It is not true that railway companies, and other business companies and private individuals having work to do, adopt the rule of letting it out by tender. On the contrary, it is quite a common thing, under the changed conditions, where we have trades unions and fixed rates of wages, to provide competent engineers and foremen, and do the work by day's labour. In this very municipality works involving ten times the amount of this work have been done by day's labour, and done with satisfaction. I take the opposite view to my hon. friends

opposite in tliis matter. I have looked into several small works, and I find that under the system of letting by tender, by the time you pay the wages of the engineer, the foremen and overseers, you find that a great deal of money is spent in that way. If a work is let by contract, even if it is a small work, the minister has to put some one in charge of it; and for that reason a great deal of public money is spent in wages of inspectors or overseers. I do not believe that the hon. gentleman will say that none but men who voted Liberal were employed. I do not believe that any such statement is correct, or that the engineer in charge had any such instruction.
I never did that in my life.
The party heeler who had charge of the work has done it.

I am prepared to deny the statement. Neither the Minister of Public Works-or any other officer in the department gave the engineer or party heelers any such instructions. A few days ago we had a similar statement made concerning another public work and made by a gentleman also living in the locality. But I have here a statement made by the contractor. Mr. Green, under his signature, giving such statements unqualified denial.
Is the hon. gentleman going to lay the letter on the Table ?

Yes, if my hon. friend wishes it. I wish to read this statement as showing how misleading and unfounded these charges are. I am sure that no member of the House is so unfair as to try and make some thing appear to exist which has no existence in reality. Notwithstanding our party feeling, surely we want these works to go on and the money to be expended to the best advantage ; and, if, instead of these carping and unfounded criticisms, hon. gentlemen would offer suggestions, the Minister pf Public Works would be only too happy to take advantage of any suggestions by which improvements in the works could be effected.
Cross the House and we will tell you how.

From the spirit the hon. gentleman exhibits, I do not think he would be very competent to be placed in the position of Minister of Public Works. I shall not read the whole of this letter of Mr. Green, but only a part of it. Mr. Green says :
Mr. Ingram is reported to have made the following statement : A London man was given the sub-contract for the brickwork. I wish to give this the most unqualified denial.
Is the hon. gentleman denying what an hon. member said ?
Yes, and this denial is signed by the contractor himself.
I submit, Mr. Chairman, that the hon. gentleman is not in order. He has no right to do so.
I do not know of any rule that will prevent me from submitting facts in contradiction of a statement made in this House.
The hon. gentleman has no right to read any document from any outsider denying any statement made by a member in this House.

I presume that the hon. member for Elgin (Mr. Ingram) made the statement from information he received, and would be glad to know the truth. If he were here, I do not believe that he would raise the point of order. The charge was made that none but supporters of the government are employed on these works. How is the House to know the truth of such charges if we are not to be allowed to give the statements of the only people who have personal knowledge. I do not think I am out of order.
The hon. gentleman is not out of order.

Mr. Green goes on to say :
He is also reported to have stated : ' It was current report in St. Thomas that Mr. Green could not get the contract until he gave a pledge that the brickwork would be given to a prominent London Liberal.' I wish also to deny this, and I am surprised that Mr. Ingram would take up the time of the House in making such statements, when he could have so easily ascertained the true facts of the matter. But I suppose this would not have suited his purpose. I might relieve Mr. Ingram's anxiety with reference to Conservatives being employed in connection with the building of the armoury, by telling him that Dr. Wilson has frequently stated that he had no objection to their being employed on any part of the works, and that in my negotiations for sub-contract I have stipulated that all available labour in St. Thomas should be employed, irrespective of politics.
The fact is that tbe contractor is a Con- -servative, and in giving the sub-contract, which I suppose he had the right to do, to a responsible man and the lowest tenderer, he made this provision, in consideration of the local feeling, that all labourers in St. Thomas, irrespective of politics, should be given a chance of employment. This shows how groundless such statements are. I have no doubt that if we had the pay-list of this work now being discussed, we would find on it many friends and supporters of the hon. gentleman who has just spoken.

The hon. the minister said that he called for tenders and got none. There was good reason why he did not receive any. I know a prominent pier and

wharf builder in the county who has built a number of public works, and is well qualified, and he told me that he would not tender. On my asking him why, he said that the government had made an appropriation to carry the local elections and did nothing, and now they were naming appropriations to carry the Dominion elections, and he had no time to fool away on such business. As the hon. member for Bothwell (Mr. Clancy) said, it was the duty of the minister, if he was going to make an expenditure of $20,000, to have advertised again for public tenders for so large a work. The minister without portfolio suggests that I am opposing the work. I never made" such a suggestion. The government deserves credit for having taken up the matter, but should also show good business administration by letting this work by tender instead of giving it to a party heeler to carry on by days' labour. I put a question on the Order paper, in order to clear the Minister of Railways, just after the last local elections. Letters were carried around in this very polling division, purporting to have come from the Minister of Railways, saying that a vote for the local government supporters would assist in obtaining a grant for a breakwater. Such were the influences used, and if report be true the party who is in charge of the work now is one of the parties who carried these letters around.

We always submit with great humility and proper respect to the ruling of the Speaker, but I desire, because it is important, to draw the attention of the Chairman to Sir John Bourinot's opinion on the point I raised. It will be found on page 408 of the second edition of his work :
Nor is it in order to read articles and newspapers, letters and other communications, whether printed or written, emanating from persons outside of the House and referring to or commenting on or denying anything said by a member, or expi'essing any opinion reflecting on proceedings within the House.

I was not reflecting on our proceedings, but simply giving some facts. An hon. gentleman got up and made certain statements which the Minister of Public Works denied, and I was giving information to show that what the Minister of Public Works said was well founded. I was producing evidence to prove the denial of the minister to be correct.

The statement was not one based on the personal knowledge of the hon. member who made it, and it was open to any other hon. member to produce such evidence as he might have to contradict that statement. The quotation used by the hon. member for Bothwell appears, to a certain extent, to contradict the decision I gave, and I would not like now to make any further positive ruling. Should the point come up
again, when I have the honour to occupy the Chair, I may be in a better position to give more particular reasons.

If I understood the Minister of Public Works correctly, he argued that it was better to have work done by day's labour than by contract; and, in, support of that contention, he said that in the great harbour of Montreal work was being done by day's labour to-day. I think the hon. minister must be aware that in a great city, where the labour unions have been asking that the work be done by day's labour and where there is a great deal of labour in the market, there might be some justification for it, where competent men can be got to oversee the work. But I think he will scarcely contend that tnat establishes the principle for other places.
I did not say that; I did not lay down any rule. I say that there are cases where work can be better carried on by day's labour, and there are other cases where it is better to ask for tender.

I understood the hon. minister to go on and support that by saying that it is a common occurrence for the government to find a contractor who is weak financially and who gives them a great deal of trouble, and that he avoided that trouble by having the work done by day's labour. He and other hon. members on that side, including the hon. member for North Oxford (Hon. Mr. Sutherland) seem to forget that some years ago, when they were in opposition, they moved a resolution affirming the principle that no work for more than $5,-' 000 should be let except by contract. That motion was carried and the principle affirmed by the House. These same gentlemen now defend the principle of doing this work by day's labour. Another statement of the hon. minister in justification of this principle was that in one case he asked for tenders but received none. In that ease, he said, he went on with the work by day's labour. But he did not say anything to show that the work was urgent and that he could not wait to ask for tenders a second time. On the other hand, there was another case mentioned in which the work was left undone for two years, a work quite as important as this other. He did not do that by day's labour, but waited until he was able to let a contract. Nobody will contend that work can be done as successfully by day's labour as by contract, when it involves a large amount. The hon. member for North Oxford came to the support of the hon. Minister of Public Works, but, in doing so. he took the very opposite position from that which he took when he was on this side.

I think there are circumstances under which the

Minister of Public Works or any other minister would be justified in having work done by day's labour. I suppose that in every department there are officials who, when a job is to be let, make calculations as to the cost; and, if the tenders are for amounts above what the job is really worth, the government would be justified in refusing to give the work to any tenderer. It is only right that the government should watch over the interests of the people and not allow a number of keen contractors to take advantage of this country. But I do say that if the government, when they undertake to do work by day's labour, should not give instructions to the man in charge of the work that none but the supporters of the government are to be employed-
I never did that.

If they did that, it would be an iniquity. No man should be prevented from earning a day's wages because of his politics; and if there is any man on the work who does not earn his money, no matter what his politics, he should be discharged.

I have just this very day been caught by the principle so strongly advocated by my hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule). We require a large quantity of coal for these public buildings here in Ottawa. The contractor who supplied the coal last year offered to supply the coal for the coming season for $5.00 a ton. But the amount of money involved is a large one-$25,000 and more ; and I said to my officers : Let us ask for tenders for this supply of coal. The tenders came in on Saturday; and, instead of getting coal from Mr. Heney by private tender for $5.00, I find that the lowest tender is $0.20. I am going to lose $2,700 for the sake of principle. If I had been directing my own affairs as a business man-as I am, I think-I would have said : This private offer is at the lowest price I can get, and I will take it. But, we have the system of public tenders, and, in this case, I followed it. Still, why should I be scolded, why should I be scarified for following my own judgment where I think money could be saved by that system ? I am not going to pay the money out of my own pocket. In this case I acted upon a so-called principle where, in fact, there is no fixed principle.

What is to hinder the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Tarte) from accepting the offer of $5.60 mow7 ? Merely because he has asked for tenders, he is not bound to accept one of those tenders. Or, ! why could he not have ascertained the price of coal in the first place-that would not be ! difficult-and then decline to pay any but a j fair price.
In other words, the system of the lowest tenderer is no good ?
Not at all.
You ask for tenders and demand a deposit-and when you have gone through all that formality you go back and accept a private offer.
Oh, oh.

It means that. Should I be justified in asking for tenders if I am to go back to a private bargain again ? I say this much- that a minister of the Crown should not be looked upon all the time as a thief; there is no sense in that. What does it benefit me to carry on work by day's labour. It does not give me a dollar, but it does give me trouble. I wish to carry out works by day's labour whenever it is best to do so. But I know how it is with hon. gentlemen opposite. I have been long enough in public life to know that when you are in opposition you find fault with everything. But 1 must say that I think that that is not a good thing to do. Because, a party does not remain for ever in opposition. And, when an opposition comes into power, if they have gone too far when on the left of the Speaker, they find themselves in a most uncomfortable position when they cross the floor. My hon. friend has gone too far. Of course the hon. gentlemen opposite may [DOT]not always remain there, doubtless they will come over to this side at some period. But I say they are going too far, they are flaying down a doctrine that no government should be asked to carry out. I do not ask to be dispensed from asking for tenders, nothing of the kind; I am only asking to be treated fairly as any other business man.

I may suggest to the minister, with whom I have a good deal of sympathy, that the fact that he was able to buy coal privately for $5.60 and found, when he asked for tenders, that the price was very much higher, might have suggested to ham that a combine had beeu formed by the coal dealers. If, a combine was formed, and I should think that would be prima facie evidence that a combine had been formed, it would be his duty as a minister of the government utterly to decline to accept any of those tenders, to return the parties their cheques, and to inquire in Montreal, Toronto or other place, as to what was the price of coal. If I were Minister of Public Works, or minister of any other department, I would not for one instant allow the government to be victimized in that manner. I think if he could buy coal at the price he indicates, and found when tenders were called for that a price greatly in advance was being asked, that

should have indicated to him that a combine was formed.

As an evidence that there was no combine, I may mention that all the prices were different. There was no combine in this case at all. The hon. gentleman would find it difficult, if he were minister in a department, first to make a private bargain, and then ask for tenders and to refuse to accept the lowest tender. He would never be able to carry on public business in that manner. Speaking in a general way, 1 think a minister should be allowed some latitude, he should be allowed to act as any business man would do under similar circumstances.

X agree with the hon. gentleman that criticism to be at all useful must be fair. Now the hon. gentleman first sets up an idol and then falls down and worships it and asks us to worship it. He says that the opposition contends that no work can be done profitably by day's labour. No such contention is made on this side of the House, consequently his argument is not called for. It has been admitted on this side that there are cases in which day's work might be justified. But the hon. gentleman goes further, and endeavours to make it appear to this committee that under all circumstances day's labour is a better system than contract. We admit that when the Conservatives were in power they had the same trouble with regard to straw men being put up to make tenders, and with regard to men failing. But the hon. gentleman's friends contended, and they were perfectly right, that every work ought to be let by tender unless it was of a trivial nature. The hon. Minister of Public Works now dissents from that principle. The member for West Elgin (Mr. Robinson) says that a minister who will give instructions that a public work shall be given only to political friends, does wrong. The minister jumps up and protests vigorously that he never gave instructions of that kind. I tell the hon. gentleman that members on this side can bring case after case where that is being done, whether by his instructions or not. If it is done without his instructions, and he is aware of it, he is just as guilty as if he had directed it to be done. I ask the hon. gentleman, if we are able to show him a case where that is being done, will he take steps to have it corrected ?

It wrould be very lamentable if a poor man was excluded from working on a public-work simply because he had voted against the government. I would never give such instructions myself. Of course I would give the preference to my political friends, all things being equal, and hon. gentlemen opposite would do the same thing. The hon. member for Bothwell (Mr. Clancy) must remember that I have been longer in public
life than he has, and I know that this principle has always been followed in this country by the Conservative party when they were in power, they always did exactly what 1 am doing now. I think, perhaps, they went even farther than we are going. For twenty years I was a member of the Conservative party, and I know that they followed the very same policy the Liberals are following now. I do not say that the Conservative party have always excluded Liberals from getting employment on a public work, and we are not doing that either. I could point out in this very building dozens and dozens of Conservatives who voted against us during the last election, and they are not interfered with.
How do you know ?

They do not hide their views. I do not try to terrorize anybody, I am not such a small man as that. My officers are fully entitled to their private opinions on political matters, and provided they serve me faithfully, I do not ask them how they voted. I know there are in the public buildings at Ottawa dozens upon dozens of men, even in the Public Works Department, who voted against the government. I have not dismissed them, nor will I do so. They are free citizens to vote as they please, provided they do not manifest open and offensive partisanship. Now I say that it is not only the right but the duty of any government to put in office their own friends in preference to others. I shall do so, and no fair man, whether Conservative or Liberal, will blame me for it. As to excluding poor workingmen from employment on government works, well, a party does not gain much by doing that. It is not my policy, and I do not do it. I give the preference to our friends, but I recommend giving employment to dozens of men who have voted against us. I know it is the best way to get them the next time.

I am very sorry that the hon. gentleman is so sensitive to criticism. He seems to think that all our criticism is personal towards himself, because, when hon. gentlemen on this side of the House undertake to criticise certain acts of the department presided over by the hon. gentleman, he seems to think that we believe that they are all thieves.
No.
The hon. gentleman said so.
I was not speaking of myself.

It may be easy for the hon. gentleman to fall among thieves, and we wish to prevent any danger of that character. We were pointing out that it would

be very much better if large works of this character were let by tender. I understand enough about these matters to know that there are certain works where it is much more to the public advantage that the principle of days' work should be adopted, and [ have no doubt that if you have always the right man as foreman the system of days' work is the best one. But, there is a very great difficulty in getting the right man. Now, it seems to me that the difficulty about weak tenderers can be very easily avoided. If the forfeit of 10 per cent is not sufficient make it a larger amount. Make it so that the forfeit will be sufficient to pay the back wages of the poor labouring men, and sufficient to prevent the public from being defrauded by means of the tenderers not being able to carry out the work. Men will not take contracts for works about which they are absolutely ignorant. These men usually know what they are undertaking when they take these contracts, and there will always be a sufficient amount kept back to protect the public interest. Certainly there is if the tenderer happens to be a Conservative. I do not know how it is when he happens to be a Grit. So long as we have party government in this country I am quite willing to acknowledge that the party in power should give their favours to their own friends. I have no fault to find with that principle, but when it comes down to a question of day's work, I think it is a small piece of business to ask a man how he is going to vote. In general, these things should go to the friends of the party in power, and there will be no criticism from this side of the House. Criticism, as far as I am concerned, is not personal towards the hon. minister himself. I consider him to be a very energetic minister. I do not think he does everything that is right, by a long shot, but the hon. minister has many good points all the same.

In regard to the hon. gentleman's complaint of our criticism and that it has been carried on unfairly, I say that criticism is always justified when a minister departs from a well-understood sound principle, as has been done in this case. That was his failure to let a contract for a $20,000 work but to undertake to do it by day's labour. It was not justified by the urgency of the situation, or by any circumstance that necessitated immediate action. In regard to the tenders that the hon. gentleman received for coal, there was one element that might go to throw light upon the question. Coal might have gone up in price in the meantime, or there may have been an understanding among the tenderers, as we know there was between the tenderers for binder twine. The tenders were all different for binder twine, but they all understood each other, and they were tendering with the same understanding. Why do you put a notice in each ten-

der that the lowest or any tender will not necessarily be accepted ? It Is because you are able to ascertain what are proper values, and if you find the prices quoted away above these values you are not bound to accept any of the tenders submitted.
We always do so.

It is for that reason. As long as we direct our criticism against any department which has violated a well-understood principle in the letting of contracts, I do not think that the hon. gentleman should complain that the criticism is unfair.
I did not complain of any unfairness-very far from it. We are discussing a very interesting point.
Why did the minister say that it would seem as if hon. members on the other side of the House thought that every man in the Public Works Department was a thief ?
No, I spoke in a general way. I am very much afraid that I am not as much of a scholar in the English language as I am in the French language.
Then, you must think in the French language and express yourself in English.

I do not always make myself clearly understood. perhaps. I do not take what is said as any personal unfairness to me, not by any means. I believe I am treated fairly by the House. I have not a word to say about that, but what I say is that I believe it is very wrong to discuss questions of that kind just as if the minister intended to do wrong. I have not known many ministers who intended to do wrong, in my long experience.

lit is amusing to hear hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House whining and lecturing the government and hon. members on this side of the House, because the government are doing in some cases, not in as many cases as they should, I think, just what hon. gentlemen opposite were doing for eighteen years. Surely, they should have more manliness than to whine day after day in this House because the government give a preference, when all things are equal, to their friends. On this question of day labour I do not hesitate to say that in nearly all cases, of course, except in large contracts, in the interest of the department, in the interest of the government, in the interest of the public, and in the interest of the labouring classes of the community, the

system of day labour is very much preferable to that of tender and contract. Tbe contractors of this country are smart men ; their chief idea, when they get a contract, is to make as large an amount of money out of it as it is possible. No one can find fault with them for that. They get their contract, and then they try to get their materials as cheaply as they can. They get the cheapest and often inferior materials for public works, and when they have secured them they will employ the labouring men of the country, they will give them starvation wages and grind them down to the very lowest figures. What protection have the government ? All the government can do is to appoint a supervisor or foreman to watch the contractor. The foreman in any locality, under present conditions, cannot be a better man than the overseer, or clerk of works, or foreman that the minister selects to oversee work done under day's labour, and he is usually the best man to be got in the community. Take a work costing $5,000 and have it done by a contractor, have the same work done under a competent overseer or foreman by day's labour, and when that work is finished it will be worth 25 per cent more to the government than if it were finished by a contractor, and the labourer will get fair wages. Under the day labour system men are hired by the government, or tbe foreman who is acting for the resident engineer, and he will give every man a fair wage. If you give the work to a contractor, he will go anywhere to get a man who will work cheaply, and he will provide inferior material. The government get very poor value from the contractor. Take the question of frauds on the government; if you look over the history of the public works in this country for the last twenty-five or thirty years, you will find that in every case where the department has been cheated or any fraud has been committed on the government, it has been done through a contractor, or through a contract given as a result of tender. In every case where work is done by day's labour you will find that an honest man undertakes to carry out the instructions of a resident engineer and in some cases, although it may cost a little more, the government will get better value, so that, in the interest of the government, in the interest of the public, and in the interest of the labouring men of this country, the system of day's labour is a good one.

If what the hon. gentleman (Mr. Mclsaac) has said were borne out by the facts, it would be a very nice thing, but unfortunately it is not so. If the person who had control of the work tried to secure the most competent men to take charge, irrespective of any consideration but to do- best for the interests of the country, the picture drawn by the hon. gentleman 110
(Mr. Mclsaac) would be a true picture. But, what are the facts ? The work is given in charge to some political heeler, whether he knows anything about the work or not.
No, no.
I say that is the actual fact.
I say no.
Irrespective of the fact whether he has anything more than a superficial knowledge, but having no expert knowledge.

WTould the hon. gentleman allow me a moment; we are discussing this in a friendly way. My instructions to the resident engineers are to accept as foremen only men who know their trade. Every time I have learned that these instructions were not carried out I have dismissed the men. I am standing in my place here, and I ask any hon. gentleman to quote a single instance of where practical men have not been employed. My orders are positive, that in every case a practical carpenter or builder shall be employed. Let me know if these orders have not been carried out.

The hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Tarte) admits that his cardinal principle is to employ his political friends. Suppose the minister found that a good Grit did not possess the necessary expert knowledge, would he discharge him and employ an expert man in the neighbourhood who was a Conservative partisan ?
I would employ him in a minute.
Under the rules of parliament we are bound to accept that statement made by the minister.
I have done it several times already.
I will accept that statement in the parliamentary sense, but, beyond that, I will reserve judgment.
I have a case in mind. I have employed in Shippegan a man who was an opponent of ours. The hon. gentleman is right when he says we must employ good foremen, and there are good foremen in our ranks.
They are scarce, but you have some of them.
I employ them, but if I am not able to find in place a Liberal foreman, I would certainly employ a Conservative, and why not ?

Why not ? Just on the very principle laid down by the minister, namely, that the work must go to his political friends. The hon. gentleman from Antigonish (Mr. Mclsaac) has spoken about whining from this side of the House. It is not a courteous term, and it is not true of the very proper criticism which has come from this side of the House. I do not believe that the majority of members on his own side will give their adherence to the principles which he has enunciated ; that it is best to carry on these public undertakings by day's work. He says tne contractors of this country are smart men, but his idea of a smart man is a very different idea from mine. I do not consider that a smart man is a dishonest man, and the hon. gentleman (Mr. Mclsaac) has made an accusation against the contractors of this country which I, for one, do not believe is borne out by the facts. I know many of the contractors of this country, and I know them to be honest, honourable men, who would not be guilty of the acts imputed to them. He says that as soon as they get a contract that their first object is to make money. Well, that is a -very worthy and laudable object. It is the object of most of us to make money or to spend it. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Mclsaac) says that the contractor then tries to get the cheapest and most inferior material. I do not believe that. There may be some dishonest contractors, just as there are dishonest men in other lines of business. Why, even the clerical profession is not exempt from them, and my own, what I call the highest profession in the country, is not exempt. But the great majority of the contractors are honest men, who fulfil to the very letter the terms of their contract, and who put in the material required by their contract. I believe the Minister of Public Works will bear out that statement in respect to the contractors of this country. But, suppose they did not put in the material required by their contract, you have the proper officers to guard the public against fraud, and they surely do their duty. If you do the work by day's labour, our officers buy this timber, and surely they are as competent to judge of the timber supplied by a contractor as they are to judge of it when they buy it themselves.

The only point my hon. friend (Mr. Fowler) attempted to make was, that the weakness of the day's labour system was because the whole work was left in the hands of a political heeler, his assumption being that in the Liberal party we could not get competent men to do the work. That statement is' so absurd that I need not argue it. Does it not occur to the hon. gentleman. that when a contract is awarded, the only safety the government has lies in the overseer, who is usually selected from among the friends of the party in power ? There is just as much danger in having an Mr. TARTE.
incompetent overseer in one case as in the other, and there is, therefore, nothing in the point the hon. gentleman makes. I did not say the contractors of this country were dishonest men. I said they were smart men, and I do not think that term is offensive. I said their first object was to make every dollar they could out of the work, and I said in most cases they would slight the materials and slight the work, and I think most men in their occupation would do that when they have the opportunity. The only chance this government has to prevent them doing that is by appointing foremen or overseers, who must be selected from the same class of persons as the foremen under the day's labour system, who usually are selected and recommended by the party in power, under the supervision of the resident engineer. In the one case the foreman is immediately under the resident engineer as in the other. Therefore, the point sought to be made by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Fowler) does not amount to much.

That would not follow at all. The man is in a different position when he is employed by the department as clerk of works to watch the work as it is going on by the contractor. He is then in the position of a paid critic, but when he is running the show himself, he has not the same inducement to look after the work properly. Therefore, you see, even a political heeler might do better work as critic in the position of clerk of works than he would if he were looking after it as foreman of a day's labour job, having charge of it himself. I am very glad my hon. friend has so far modified his first statement as to admit
I did not modify my first statement.

My hon. friend did modify his first statement, and I am very glad that what I said caused him to do so. He first made the sweeping statement, applied to all the contractors of this country, that their object was to see how cheap and inferior material they could use in their work. Now he says he will admit that there are some contractors who are honest. I think that the Minister of Public Works will bear me out in saying that the great mass of the contractors of this country are honest, upright men.

I am sure that my hon. friend did not try to convey the idea that all the contractors were dishonest men-nothing of the kind. Since I have been in office I have had a great deal of intercourse with contractors, and I am glad to say that most of them are honest men. very honest men ; but at the same time a great many of them, honest as they mav be, try to the best of their ability

to evade the fair wages clause. Human nature is there. That is one of the reasons why I make this prophecy, for which I do not charge anything, that the day labour system will become more and more popular. Contractors at present give us a great deal of trouble. I have had complaints from the Labour Bureau in regard to several contractors who had contracts, they by one means or another evade the fair wages clause. Workmen complain of that, and we have to make inquiries to ascertain whether the workmen are right or whether the contractor is right. If we carry out a public work by day labour, with a good foreman-I must always make that condition-there will be no trouble in that re-speet. The government will pay fair wages and will buy good materials. The government do not wish to make a profit ; they have only to see that the work is properly carried out. I understand the objection raised by my hon. friends on the other side of the House. They believe that the day labour system will work to their detriment -that necessarily the party in office will employ more of their own friends than friends of the opposite party. There is something in that; but these are the fortunes of war, and they cannot affect the great principle that the workmen of this country have rights that are not always recognized by contractors, even by the best.

We do not complain so much of that as we do of letting it be known to parties who wish to get emplov-rnent that they cannot get it unless they belong to the government party. I found that to be the case in my constituency. If men were willing to support my opponent, they were not denied work.

I do not wish just now to discuss a work in my hon. friend's riding. When we come to that, he will find that under the contract system the work has not gone on satisfactorily. I will discuss that with him with pleasure when we come to the item.

I do not think there is any question in the minds of the members of this House that the Minister of Public Works understands the meaning of the word honesty very much better than the hon. member for Antigonish (Mr. Mclsaac), and I am pleased to find that the minister has not taken this discussion as a personal matter at all. Will the minister give the name of the gentleman who is performing this work at Wilson's Beach under Mr. Shewan ?
I have not the name here, but I will give it to the hon. gentleman to-night or tomorrow.

I regret that the hon. gentleman has not the name. He has stated 110*
that he will only employ men who have ability. Well, the hon. gentleman in charge of this work is a fisherman.
Will my hon. friend give me his name ?
His name is Mr. Ethel-bert Savage, unless the government has changed him since the work was started.

My instructions in this case, as in all others, have been that Mr. Shewan must not accept the services of any man whom he does not himself know to be a carpenter or builder. If he has done differently, the man will be dismissed at once, because my orders have been very positive in that respect.
Would my hon. friend give me the name of the other man ?
Does the hon. gentleman say he is not a practical man ?
His business has been that of a fisherman all his life.
I want to ask the hon. gentleman if that man is not a carpenter and builder ?
Not in the sense of building wharfs.
Will my hon. friend contend that because that man is a fisherman he is not an able man ?

Not by any means. We have the ablest fishermen in the county of Charlotte that there are in Canada. Can the minister tell me how they procure timber for this work, and who has charge of the procuring of timber ?
Mr. Shewan, the resident engineer, gives orders for the timber personally or through his agent.
Is it to be presumed that the gentleman in charge of this work would be Mr. Shewan's agent for the purchase of timber ?
The foreman will necessarily arrange, and Mr. Shewan will have cognizance of the arrangement and approve or disapprove of

Here is a location probably 100 miles from the place where the timber will have to be obtained. On the Island of Campobello there is not a stick of timber fit to go into this work. This wharf will have a face of 50 or 60 feet, as the maximum tide is about 30 feet, and it will have to be built so that a vessel can lie beside it at low water ; and to put a man in charge of such a work, costing $20,000 or $21,000, who has practically no

experience in constructing such a work, is nothing less than an outrage.

I may say that the man now appointed will not be the inspector of the work which is to go on. The acting chief engineer lias just conveyed that information to me. I can assure my hou. friend that I shall be only too glad if he gives me information of anything wrong that has been done or that may be done later on in connection with this work.

My impression, and it is one which will be gained by the people today from east to west, after the minister's speech, is that there is a sort of dual Grit Providence, consisting of the Minister of Public 'Works and the Minister of Railways, presiding over our public works and railways, which will only allow Grit partisans to get employment on those works
River St. John, Including tributaries, $16,000.
What amount is to be expended on dredging ?

No part of this will go to dredging, but will be used in building and repairing wharfs and piers. There is a general item for dredging, out of which the money required to work the little dredge we have built specially for St. John river will be supplied.

I would like to draw the attention of the hon. minister to the importance of removing those shoals. The Board of Trade at Fredericton has drawn the attention of the government on numerous occasions to the importance of that work, and I am very sorry that there is not some considerable amount voted for that purpose.

I must remind my hon. friend that we have a pretty large amount in the estimates! for dredging in New Brunswick, and out of that amount the work of dredging the St. John river will be paid.
St. John Harbour-Negro Point breakwater,

This is a large breakwater which cost half a million, and this amount of money is required especially to repair that portion of it on which the lighthouse is erected. The waves are tremendously high there and that breakwater requires yearly a large expenditure.
At six o'clock, committee took recess.
After Recess.
Committee resumed at eight o'clock.
Public Works-Chargeable to Income-Harbours and Rivers-Maritime Provinces Generally -General repairs to harbours and river works, $10,000.
Has the lion. Minister of Public Works arranged to spend any of this money for wharfs on the Kennebecasis river ?
No.

Last October, shortly before the election, a party consisting of the Liberal candidate, and several members of the local government and the local legislature made a trip through that part of my constituency and made promises that certain wharfs should be built. The hon. Minister of Public Works knows that it has been the custom, for some time past in the building of wharfs on the St. John river and its tributaries, that half the expense is borne by the local government and half by the Dominion government. A wharf was promised
By whom ?

By the then member for the county and candidate for the government-at a place called Gondola Point. I would like to ask the minister if the government intends to build a wharf there or to give any amount toward a wharf along any part of the St. John river within the county of King's ?

I did not authorize anybody to promise a wharf. If anybody went there with a promise, it was without authority of the Public Works Department. Some members of the local government may have made promises. No officers were sent there from the Public Works Department.

No officers of the department accompanied this party; but the government candidate is supposed to speak with authority on a matter of that kind. Of course, I do not wonder that the hon. *minister smiles. But I may say that the place I have referred to is a very important point, a great deal of trade being carried on there, and I trust the hon. minister will see his way clear to expend some of this vote upon wharfs on that part of the St. John and Kennebecasis rivers lying in my constituency.
This vote, as my hon. friend will see, is for repairs and improvements only. This has nothing to do with building new wharfs.

There is a vote just before this ' River St. John, including tributaries $16,000.' The Kennebecasis would be included in this as a tributary of the St. John. Where is it proposed to spend this amount ?
I may say that my hon. friend will find in the supplementary estimates a vote for wharfs of the character just mentioned.

I desire to call the attention of the minister to the necessity of dredging the St. John river at the Oromocto shoal. The Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair), having lived in Fredericton, knows the great necessity of this work. While I am on my feet, I may say that for about twenty years we have never had the honour of a visit from any Minister of Public Works to that section of the country. About twenty years ago, Sir Hector Langevin, while Minister of Public Works was there. And I may say that I do not remember seeing the chief engineer of the department there since Mr. Perley held the position fifteen or sixteen years ago. I can assure you, Mr. Chairman, that this is a most important work, and one in which the people along the river for a distance of eighty miles, including the cities of Fredericton and St. John, are very much interested. When the water is at summer level, many of the vessels that pass up and down must be partially unloaded. This places the commerce along that river in a very deplorable condition, adding very much to the cost of transport.

I should be only too glad to pay a visit to the part of the country the hon. gentleman Mr. Wilmot has referred to. When I took a trip to the maritime provinces some time ago, it was too late when I reached St. John to take a trip to Fredericton. I was very sorry not to be able to go there. My hon. friend is right-either the Minister of Public Works or the chief engineer should travel more than we do. As I said a few days ago. I am coming more and more to believe that the minister should not be loaded, as he is with, so many details. If we travelled more, we should know the country better, and that would be a benefit to the works that are going on and to the country at large. I shall take note of what my hon. friend has told us, and the chief engineer, who is in sound of my voice has taken note of it also.
Public Works-Chargeable to Income-Harbours and Rivers-Quebec-Father Point-Landing pier, $15,000.
Will that complete the works ?

No. We are asking for tenders for that work. It Is not a local work, but has been asked for by all the navigation companies of Montreal and all the pilots. This is the spot where the ocean steamers stop, and it is to my personal knowledge that steamers are obliged to wait there for hours because there is not a landing place where pilots can be taken up by the steamers or put ashore from them.
The work will be done by contract ?

Yes.
Public Works-Chargeable to Income-Harbours and Rivers-Quebec-General repairs and improvements to harbour, river and bridge works, $15,000.
The hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Tarte) is increasing this vote $5,000 over last year.

The number of works is increasing every year.. and we are obliged to ask for more money because we have more work to attend to.
Hull-Landing pier, $38,500.
Mr. CLANCY'. Is that a very extensive work ? I see that this large vote is asked in addition to $10,000 asked for last year. Is thio for the same work ?

Yes, the work is under contract, and has been awarded to the lowest tenderer.
Magdalen Islands-Breakwater, $7,000.
What shape is that in ?
The work is going on now at Amherst. This sum will complete it.
Is it performed by tender ?

No, by day labour, under an engineer.
Rivibre aux Renards-Pier, $7,000.
The MINISTER OF PUBLIC W^LlvS. This is to be placed under contract by tender.
I see $8,000 was taken last year. How much of that has been expended ?

No work has been done. The chief engineer tells me that perhaps we may require a couple of thousand more to complete the work. Anyhow, tenders will be asked for.
St. Alexis-Bais des Ha! Ha!-Pier, $4,000.
Will the minister explain that ?

That work is carried on under an old engineer, Mr. Blais, by day labour. It has already begun. In that part of the country, I may say, the day labour system has been very successful.
St. Jerome-Lake St. John-Wharf, $2,000.

This is to complete the work at that place. That district, I may say, is one of the most enterprising of the province of Quebec. New

settlers are going in there every day, and these works are being constructed for their benefit.
When was that work commenced ?
Last year, to he completed this year.
Under contract ?
No, under (the supervision of Mr. Blais, an old and trusty engineer.
I am afraid the hon. gentleman has sinned again there.

Well, if I am guilty there I am guilty all round, because all our works in that district have been carried on, under the same system. This is a new district, new settlers are pouring in there, as the hon. member for Montmorency (Mr. Casgrain) knows, I know he will justify this vote.
St. Lambert-Cribwork protection wall, $4,000.
This work is to protect the shores. The work was begun last year, and will be completed this year.
Under contract ?
No.

Now the hon. gentleman has a very large sum there again. I am sure this committee will not object to the smaller sums. It might be a proper thing to have it done by day's work, but the hon. gentle man must know that he has so widely departed from any reasonable mark that he is open to severe criticism.

I may tell the hon. gentleman that this work is under the charge of an engineer iu Montreal, Mr. Michaud, an engineer of long experience. I can assure my hon. friend that these works have been carried on cheaply, well and successfully.
Sorel-Deep water wharf, $100,000.
With respect to this item, I would like to have it stand in the absence of the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk).
I was going to ask to have this item stand myself.

I would say to the minister that I would like to have it understood that any of these items that we have passed might be discussed again on this particular one, when my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier returns.
Certainly.
J Tadousac-Repairs to wharf, $1,500.
This is to complete the work.
Perhaps the hon. gentleman could tell us so far as all these items are concerned in No. 163, just how much of the work is being done by day's labour and how much is being done by tender and contract.
I can do that.

The hon. gentleman has not given us that information in all cases as he has gone along. We have not asked for it in all cases. I think it would be more convenient to take them all together, and produce the statement on the next occasion.

I will prepare a statement.
Ontario-Cobourg-Repairs to pier and dredging, $5,000.
The pier is 450 feet long. The western face of the middle pier is 350 feet long.
Was the $5,000 voted last year all expended ?
Up to the present time $3,320 have been spent out of the amount voted last year.
Was that on the pier or for dredging the harbour ?
$659 have been spent on the pier, $1,447.70 on materials and $1,112.65 on dredging.
Have you your own dredge ?
Yes.
Is the harbour of Cobourg a private or a public harbour ?
I understand it has always been held to be a public harbour.
All these harbours are owned by private corporations.

It may be that some of them are held by private corporations, but they do not keep them up. and the government has been obliged to come to the rescue of the community.
Collingwood-Harbour improvements, $25,000.
Could the hon. minister tell us in what state of progress this work is ?

The contract for which this $25,000 is asked was entered into while I was on the

other side of the ocean, by the lion. Postmaster General (Hon. Mr. Mulock). It provides for a channel 110 feet wide and 20 feet deep at .low1 water. The contract was partially carried out during last season, with a great deal more success than the work was carried out In the previous year. Mr. Boone has a good plant now, and is carrying on the work with a good deal of success. The contract carried out so far was for the inner part of the harbour. This $25,000 and $8,000 that remains is to give the same depth and width outside.

Will the hon. minister tell us, in the first place, the length of the channel ? I understand it to be 110 feet wide. I think last year it was understood that it was to be 150 feet wide. Will the hon. minister tell us the length, and how much of it is dredged to a depth of 20 feet ?
The length of the channel, dredged to the depth of 20 feet and to a width of 110 feet, is 2,350 feet.
To what length will the channel be dredged to get to deep water ?

I understand that with the $25,000 and with the $8,000 remaining, we will dredge about 3,500 feet more of the outer part of the same channel. Of course, there is a greater depth outside than there is inside.
Will that complete the channel to deep water, 110 feet wide and 20 feet deep ?
Yes.
Is the contract let for that ?
It is practically let. We are just making arrangements to carry out the work.
What is the total cost of the work to be ?
I understood the contract was practically made ?
Yes, with Mr. Boone, whose plant is on the spot.
I understand he was much more 'successful last year than before ?
Yes.
I would like to say, in connection with this vote, that there has been a great boom in Collingwood lately, and that this is going to be a very important place.
There is a shipyard at Collingwood.

I do not think the channel is wide enough. I am told by vessel men that the channel is not wide enough for
the safety of those ironclad steamers that are expected to come there. It seems to me that it was understood originally that the width was to be 450 feet. This was reduced very much. I do not know whether I am incorrect in my memory, but I think it was understood last year that it was to he 150 feet. It appears that it has now been reduced to 110 feet. That seems to he a very narrow channel, and that incalculable injury would be done to one of these iron vessels if it should strike a rock. I am told that Mr. Boone did the work very successfully last year, and if he is able to continue it the government are likely to get as good value from him as from any one else. I presume that the work has been done on a schedule, and that the work remaining to be done will be done on the same system. I understand that you have done about 2,350 feet, and that you have 3,500 feet to do.
I was not aware that there was very much difference in the depth of the channel inside and outside.
Oh, yes.

If it be a fact that the outside 3,500 feet is about as shallow as the inside 2,350 feet of the channel, it seems to me unlikely that $32,000 will finish it, if you have spent so much on the inner channel. But, no doubt the hon. gentleman's officers have made a calculation, and there is no doubt that the engineer should know just how much it will take. In my opinion, it is a matter of great importance that the channel should be made wider, because I do not think it is a proper width for the safety of large vessels going in and out of the harbour.

I share, to a very large extent, the view expressed by the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproulel. I think that the trade of Collingwood is developing so rapidly that it will soon become necessary to widen the channel. The people of Collingwood were anxious to get a channel, and the present arrangement was entered into. We will complete the dredging of the outside channel, and I may say that the dredging is not of the same material ns that of the inside channel. It is not as hard as the dredging of the inner harbour was, and this explains why it will be completed for a little less money. When we have exhausted this sum of money, if the trade of Collingwood goes on developing, I am sure parliament will not hesitate to grant more money. I 'am glad that the hon. member for East Grey shares my view. Collingwood has been one of my pet places. I do not know why I took such a fancy to the place, but I have no doubt it was because the people

were so enterprising. They contributed their own money to this project, and I decided 1 would do what I could to help them.

When Collingwood gave, as it did, a very substantial sum for this work, the old government were committed to it, and the present government, I understand, carried it out on somewhat the same lines. The people of Collingwood have enterprise, and they are deserving of every consideration. I am glad to know that the minister appreciates it. and that as the government has undertaken the work, he intends to make it what it should be, namely, a first-class job.

I am sure the people of Collingwood fully appreciate the interest which the hon. gentleman from East Grey (Mr. Sproule) takes in Collingwood harbour. I desire to say for my part, that the Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte) deserves the gratitude of the people of Collingwood for the interest he has taken in connection with their harbour, and the other industries of the town. It is by reason of the arrangement which his department succeeded in making with the present contractor Mr. Boone, that we have such a satisfactory condition of things existing in that harbour to-day. The other contract was not working satisfactorily, but the present contract is giving great satisfaction to the peop'e of that place. The town is thriving to a very large extent, as the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) has said, and by reason of the fact that the government are going to deepen the harbour to twenty feet, we have a very large shipping establishment now in progress employing upwards of 300 men, which shows what a town on the inland waters can do if encouraged by the government. The hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) has taken a paternal interest in Collingwood, and as he has conveyed to the minister the feeling of the inhabitants, I may say that I am perhaps in a better position to do that than he is. because a couple of days before the last election the hon. gentleman appeared in Coliingwood to tell the electors that the Conservative government which he represented were entitled to credit for this work, and not the Liberal government. However, the people of Collingwood saw through the proper spectacles, and by reason of the way in which they cast their votes, I aip here to-night to express their gratitude to the government and to the Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte).

The hon. gentleman (Mr. McCarthy) is quite mistaken as to what the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Srpoule) said in Collingwood. I said that the work was undertaken by the Conservatives, and that as the present government had carried it out on the lines laid down by the Conservative government, they were eu-

titled to credit for everything they had done. I did not say a word against them for undertaking the work, but I added I had too much respect for the honesty of the present government to believe that even if their candidate were defeated they would abandon the work on that ajccount. I thought it would be carried out and successfully carried out. That is exactly what I said.*
Hear, hear.
Good for the present government.
What will be the total cost of this work ?
The total cost without this vote has been
How much would it require to complete the work according to the plans ?

These two sums, the $25,000 and the $8,000, will complete the deepening and widening of the outer channel to twenty feet. It will complete the work for the time being.
Colpoys Bay-Extension of pier, $1,400.
What work is going on there ?

The chief engineer told me that they asked $600 last year, but they found it was not sufficient to carry out the work. This work is intended to reach a depth of sixteen feet at low water, the depth now being only eight feet.
Goderich Harbour-Dredging. $7,000.
How is our friend Dan McGillicuddy getting on with this ?
It is not for McGillicuddy at all. It is to dredge the harbour.

No, not one cent of it.

No, he never had it.

No.

He had the contract to rebuild the pier.

Now, let us come in or let us come out. He got the contract because he was the lowest tenderer, and he carried it out. Public tenders were called for, and he was the lowest, and he did the work.

He did not manipulate the dredging.

Yes.
So long as he did it lower than any one else, there is no reason to complain, though he is a newspaper man.
He did it all right.
