The dredging was done at the ordinary price of $8 an hour by the Martin Dredging Co. We exact that all dredges must do 600 yards a day, which makes 13J cents a yard, which is not a dear price.
Is that the Martin Dredging Company of Chatham ?

No. of Goderich. By the way the dredging company at Chatham about which I was so severely handled without gloves by my hon. friend, have declined so far to carry out the work we have offered them, because they want to work more than ten hours a day. They say that $8 an hour for ten hours work is not enough, and I have not been able to carry out the work so far.

I may say that the Martin Dredging Company of Chatham have a splendid dredging outfit, and they do a class of dredging that is always well done. I do not think that their dredges should be classed with some of the dredges the minister is forced to use, because I am satisfied it is difficult to make a distinction in some cases. I venture to say the dredges are better than some of the government dredges, and the manager is a very enterprising man who will see that the work will be well done. I do not say that because he is a political supporter of mine, for he is not.
I am bound to say what Is right of a man who bears such a high reputation in that business.
Was this dredging work given by contract ?

We have a regular price which was not
fixed by this government, but which was fixed by the late government, namely. $8 an hour, and I have added the condition that the dredges must take out GOO yards a day. That is, 13i cents a yard. We do not pay more than that, even if they dredge more than 600 yards a day. We have an inspector who sees that all the dredges work ten hours a day.
And if they dredge 800 yards they do not get any more ?

No. I understand that it will require a small sum of money in addition to complete the work. As some of my hon. friends know, Goderich harbour probably receives the largest lake boats. Last year there were boats drawing seventeen feet of water accommodated in that harbour. One boat carried
116,000	bushels of corn, another 138,000 bushels of wheat, another 112,000 bushels of wheat. The shipping on the Georgian Bay is developing in a marvellous way, and nothing gives me more pleasure than to do this work, because its results appear immediately. As soon as deeper water is provided, additional trade at once follows.

You will require to do more yet, because some of those boats carry as much as 250,000 bushels of corn. I do not object to the expenditure, but I wish to know how much will be required to provide the depth of water needed ?

I think $7,000 or $8,000 additional will be required to complete the work.
Ontario-General repairs and improvements to harbour, river and bridge work, $15,000.

This might be a proper place for me to inquire of the hon. Minister of Public Works if he remembers a river called the Sydenham, for which there was a vote last year and the year before, and also a place which the hon. gentleman did the people the honour of visiting, called Little Bear Creek. I notice that both of these have disappeared mysteriously from the estimates.
My hon. friend will find that vote in the supplementary estimates. All the revotes are there ?

They are not in yet. Has the hon. gentleman another batch ? I looked very anxiously, because I know the Minister of Public Works desired to carry on those works, but I was doomed to disappointment. I hope he will now make two statements-first, that he will pub the vote in the estimates, and next that he will spend the money.

My hon. friend will find in the supplementary estimates the same amount as was

The contract has been awarded only a month ago, so no money has been spent so far. The contract has been given to the lowest tenderer.
What is the amount of the contract ?

John Flock, of Chatham.

Meaford Harbour-Dredging and pile work, $41,000.

The amount of the contract is $62,570. It was awarded to the lowest tenderer, Mr. Piggott, of Hamilton. He started work, and found that the material was a great deal harder than he anticipated. His plant, I believe, was not a very good one, and the work did not proceed to the satisfaction of the Department of Public Works and the public. I urged the contractor as well as I could, and lately we have notified him in a very positive manner that he is to carry out his contract, or it will be taken from him and the deposit confiscated. We have given him a writen notification to that effect. I find that Mr. Piggott is bound to lose money on that contract ; but it as his fault. He Should have made borings, and he would have found that the material, instead of being the ordinary hard material, was the hardest that a contractor could face. But all the same he has signed his contract, he has taken his chance, and he has to work it out as best he can. The work has to go on. I am sorry that has taken place, because I know that there is a Chicago company which has undertaken to erect an elevator there and bring down a large quantity of grain. The Grand Trunk Railway have also undertaken to change their station and bring it down to the harbour. I trust that our hopes will materialize and that Mr. Piggott will carry out his work. If not I will confiscate his deposit and take the best means possible to carry out the work. If instead of having a contract. the work had been undertaken by the department under supervision of an able engineer, it would have been completed now. The public and the community will suffer a great deal because that man met with Mr. TARTE.
difficulties he did not anticipate. He tried to avoid his contract, but I would not allow him, although to carry it out may ruin him. I understand that he is fairly well off but not a man of large means. He stands to lose a very large amount of money by his contract. The contract was signed on the 15th June, 1900, and is to be completed by the 15th December, 1901. Of course we have not reached the 15tli December, 1901. but I am very much afraid the work will not be completed by that time.

There was much active work going on during the election. Mr. Piggott was there. He was the contractor for the harbour works and for extending the railway down to the wharf and for the elevator. He had a large number of men on the spot, and some of the people of the vicinity were uncharitable enough to say that the object was rather for the benefit of the Minister of Public Works than the public interest. There were three dredges at work, one brought from Owen Sound, one of the owners of which was the hon. member for North Grey (Mr. Horsey). It would have looked bad to have found that dredge employed in the constituency for which that hon. gentleman was running as a member. During the election time, this was one of the most lively places, and work was progressing very rapidly. Of course all this rather reduced my majority. I told the people that I did not blame the Minister of Public Works because the place required it, and I was glad to see him making the expenditure, and that in the end it would be all right, as the result would be that the people would get the harbour and the minister's candidate defeated.
The work is a very important one. Meaford harbour has this advantage that withiu a few feet of the end of the dock you have any depth of water you require. From 75 to 100 feet to the outside, there is a depth of 25 to 30 feet, so that the largest vessels from the upper lakes will be able to come in without difficulty when this work is done. Then there is a magnificent elevator just about completed, and the Grand Trunk Railway have extended their road down to the elevator. While Collingwood cannot accommodate these large vessels which are bringing heavy loads of grain. Meaford can. and both are supplied by the Grand Trunk Railway. There is a level road from Meaford to Collingwood and from Collingwood to Toronto, and while Collingwood cannot be used for handling grain Sleaford can be successfully used for that purpose. When the elevator is finished, there will be splendid accommodation for loading and discharging vessels. Meaford has given very liberally to get this accommodation. I think she gave $30,000 to extend the railway down to the dock and into the elevator and $25,000 to the elevator, so that this small place has given $60,000 for these purposes. I
I

only ask /the minister to see that the contract is carried out as it was let.
Yes.

If the contract was let in too great a hurry, no doubt the minister was excusable, as the elections were coming on. The whole thing was done in haste and Mr. Piggott may repent at leisure. 1 believe he is a comparatively wealthy man and has been doing his work fairly well, but it is progressing very slowly of late. Had he continued with the same activity as he displayed last fall, the work would be completed by this.

Mr. Piggott can not go on with the plans he has now and must procure other plans and change his methods. Otherwise he can not possibly carry out his work. He has to dredge in very hard material indeed. My hon. friend complains that the contractor was very active during the elections.
I am not complaining ; I am satisfied.

I am not displeased myself. My hon. friend is an old member of parliament. Had he been defeated perhaps we would not have been sorry, but personally I would have missed him in the House. He is an old parliamentarian and men of his character are valuable in the House. I am very glad to have him here now.
Owen Sound Harbour-Dredging and extension of pile protection works, $8,500.

I have heard complaints in Owen Sound that this important harbour was not being dealt with liberally enough. Perhaps the hon. gentleman may supplement this grapt by something in the supplementary estimates.
Public Works-Chargeable to Income-Harbours and Rivers-Ontario-Point Peelee Island -Wharf, $2,500.
Will that work be completed during the present season ?
We expect it will be completed this season. The contract has been awarded to Mr. Clarke of Wiarton for $7,440.
The hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Tarte) got a vote of $6,000 last year, and this added to the vote of this year will make more than $7,440.

We are asking $1,000 for superintendence and contingencies.
Port Burwell-Improvement to harbour, $23,000.
Will this complete the work ?
This will be enough to complete the work, but it will not be completed this year.
There is a railway to Port Burwell, and they expect to do a large business. It is important that this work should be completed.
I think the work has been carried on very satisfactorily by Mr. Teall. He is a competent man and we trust him.
Is this under contract ?
No, it is work of repairs.
The hon. minister had $30,000 last year, and now he is asking for $23,000. Is he going to use all this on one work without a contract 1

Yes, and it is being done very successfully. If the hon. member for East Elgin (Mr. Ingram) were here, he would tell the hon. gentleman that the work was being carried on most successfully. I may say that I am accused of not having carried it out with the political zeal that my hon. friend (Mr. Ingram) accused me of.
I do not see anything here for Port Stanley. I suppose the hon. minister will see to that ?

Yes, there is something here for Port Stanley-to complete the work of dredging.
Providence Bay-Wharf, $1,300.
I see that there was a vote of $7,000 last year.
Yes, the work is under contract with Messrs. A. F. Bowman & Porter of Southampton. They were the lowest tenderers-$7,500; and there is $854 for printing, advertising, superintendence, &c.
And this completes the work ?
Yes.
What depth of water will this give ?
It does not appear in my notes, nor can the chief engineer inform me. But a note will be made of the point, and the information brought down.
You expect to complete the work this year ?

Yes.

Rondeau Harbour-Dredging, $5,000.

Has the contract been let for this work ? I understand the Chatham Dredging Company, at the head of which is Mr. Martin, to whom I referred a moment ago, had the work, or a portion of it last year. Has the contract been let for the coming season ?
South Nation River-Towards improvements at the pitchoff, $5,000.
What work is being done there ?
We are deepening the river to prevent floods.
Is it likely to be successful ?

The Chatham Dredging Company did part of the work last year, and did it very successfully. They are a good company. This year, we have a dredge of our own which wintered there. It will work first at Port Stanley and will then be sent to Rondeau. But I intend to employ the Chatham Dredging Company in the Thames river first. I suppose they will work under the usual conditions that we exact of all the companies. In point of fact, I have instructed the chief engineer to tell the company to start work immediately on the Thames river on the usual conditions.
Yes. Mr. Tait has telegraphed me that when the big floods came this year the work has shown to be very successful. There is a part of the river further down that has not been dredged.
I was down there last year, and I found that people in the locality seemed to think that, unless dredging was done further down, the work would not be successful.

I intend to make a full study of the question during the recess.
Rondeau Harbour-To complete repairs to pier,
Is that under contract ?

No, it is carried out by our own engineer. It is a work of repairs. I visited the work myself. It would have been next to impossible to take a contract, because, when you start you never know what work is to be done. You take up one piece of timber thinking it will be the last, but you find you have to go deeper and take others.
I see that $9,500 was voted last year. How much of this was spent ?
From the 1st July to the 31st December, 1900, the amount spent was $6,519.
Can the hon. gentleman say what the work will cost when completed ?

The chief engineer tells me that the amount now asked for will complete the work.
Mr. CLANCY*. Will it be completed this year ?
The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS, Yes.
Sheguiandah-Landing pier, $3,300.
This is under contract.
I see that $3,300 was voted 'last year in addition to the $3,300 this year. What was the amount of the contract ?
The contract is for $5,900 ; with $832 for printing, advertising, superintendence. &c.
Toronto harbour-Works at eastern entrance, &c., $22,000.
Will the minister kindly inform the committee if this sum of $22,000 is all he intends to spend on Toronto harbour this year ?

This sum of money is for a special object, as the hon. gentleman sees, to complete the work at the eastern entrance. We are lengthening that pier so as to prevent the filling up as much as possible. Toronto harbour is one of the most difficult harbours to protect; the current, instead of going from west to east, goes in the other direction ; it is not a fast current, but still there is a current. When a wreck takes place, and any one is drowned, we have found that it is always on the western end. The engineers are all of the opinion that the extension of the pier will have a good effect. The hon. gentleman asks me whether this amount is all the government intend to put in the estimates. Will he permit me to ask him to have a little patience ? When the supplementary estimates come before us. we will deal with that very item. The main estimates only contain votes for expenditure on works already begun. When the supplementary estimates come before us- well, I hope we will not quarrel.
Will the sum mentioned here complete the work ?

We will probably be obliged to ask a revote in the supplementary estimates of the money contained in these estimates, because we will not be able to spend, up to the 1st of July, all the amounts that are included in this year's estimates, but with these amounts we will complete the work of the eastern entrance.

Wiarton-Landing pier, $4,500.
What was the result of the hon. minister's inspection at the time he got stuck in the snow up there V

The result was very disastrous indeed. I verily believe that if I had not been blocked at that time the result might have been different. However, I have had many reverses in my life, and they have not killed me. There is only one thing that I have to complain of, and that is that the Grand Trunk Railway station is a very poor one, I found life very lonesome and uncomfortable that day ; and I came down to Ottawa very sick, politically and bodily.
The people will not com plain if the minister only carries out his intention, and makes the improvements he intimated to them were very desirable.

I intimated that the port of Southampton is a very important one, and I believe it. We were defeated in that constituency, and I would have been more pleased if we had carried that election, but it will not make any difference. I believe that Southampton is one of the most important harbours in that part of the country, and I believe that something must be done there.
Lake Manitoba-Opening of additional outlets to prevent overflow of lake, $5,000.

One or two sessions ago a considerable discussion took place upon an item for this same service. Now the hon. gentleman is asking sums of money, not for the work of lowering the lake, but for a work, I understand, that is partly of a drainage character. Perhaps the hon. gentleman could give us full information at this time.

The contract was awarded on the 22nd of December, 1898, to Mr. Lemoine, of Montreal, for the sum of 527,500. The contractor did not succeed very well at the beginning, he did not seem to understand the nature of the work. But, be has been doing very well since, and my engineer tells me that the work will be completed in about a month. This sum will complete the work.
Wharf on Lake Winnipeg, $3,400.
What work is that ?
This amount of money is to complete the work at Gimli.
Is that contract work ?

It was contract work ; but, God only knows, and myself, the trouble I had with it. There were two wharfs under contract on that
lake, the wharf at Gimli and the wharf at Geyser. In both cases the contractor did not carry out his work, and we were obliged to complete it by day labour, after having all the trouble that decent men should not be subjected to.
British Columbia-Columbia River-Improvements above Golden, $5,000.
What is the nature of these improvements, and how much will it take to complete ?
Columbia river is a very important river, and this is specially for the purpose of dredging, removing boulders and sand. We have a dredge of our own there, which is working well.	*
Are these works being carried on year after year ?

Yes. New sand bars and obstacles of that nature are forming every year.
Fraser River-Improvement of channel, protection works, &c., $10,000.
Is that under contract ?
No.
What did you do with the vote of $55,000 voted last year ?

We did not spend much last lear, we spent about $24,000. I think I will give some explanation about that work, and take the committee into my confidence. When we took office there had been a large amount of money expended on the Fraser river. The same kind of work that had been carried out on the Fraser river was tried there, that is to say, mattrasses were sunk to make a channel in the river. When we started there was about 12 feet of water. By the use of these mattrasses the Public Works Department made a channel. The water was raised to over 20 feet. Unfortunately the Fraser river is such a powerful and treacherous stream that our works were overpowered. There is a rise at times of 60 feet. I have practically given up hope of maintaining these works. We are trying to maintain Western Island. We have protected it with these mattrasses so as to keep the channel as straight as possible. I had made up my mind to fight against all powerful nature, but, after reflection, after having given a great deal of consideration to this question, I have come to the conclusion that it is better to wait and not to expend any large sums of money now. If the trade of New Westminster and of the country above that point develops, something may have to be done, but I feel I would not be justified in asking from my colleagues and from parliament a continuation of the

large expenditure that was incurred in the past. That is the reason why I am asking this year only a moderate sum of money.
I understand you have only spent $2,600 ?
Is it intended to spend the balance of the $55,000 in that same work ?

No, I have made up my mind not to spend much money this year. The Public Works Department which began that work ten years ago has not been successful with it. The Fraser river is probably the most difficult river in the world to deal with. I do not expect to spend more than $10,000 to protect Western Island.
Skeena river, $6,500.
What is that for- dredging ?

This is a very important river for the canneries. Large quantities of salmon are caught there and we have every year to remove snags and obstacles from the river.
Dredge Vessels-Repairs, $30,000.
This amount of money is asked every year and spent every year for repairs to dredges and it will apply all over Canada.
How many dredges does the department own ?

In the maritime provinces, we have the St. Lawrence, the Cape Breton, the Prince Edward, the George McKenzie, the Canada, the New Clam Shell dredge, which has no name, and the tug Cricket. In Quebec and Ontario we have the Challenge and tug, the Queen and tug, the St. Louis and tug, the Nipissing and tug, the Ontario and tug, Canals No. 1 and tug. We have in Manitoba, the dredge Quebec, the tug Sir Hector and two coal barge scows. In British Columbia, we have the dredge Mudlark and tug and the snag boat Samson with scows. These dredges have to be kept in order every year. I am forgetting that we have dredges on Lake St. John, on the St. Maurice river and on the river St. John, N.B.
What kind of repairs are necessary ? Are these vessels injured in the service ?
There are a great many breakages.
Could the hon. minister tell me where these vessels are employed in the maritime provinces ? Take one of them, the St. Lawrence, for instance.

The Cape Breton has been working in St. John during the last three seasons helping to dredge the harbour. The St. Lawrence, was engaged last year in the St. Mary's river. The dredge Canada has been working in Yarmouth during the last two or three seasons. The George McKenzie has been working at different places and is now at Port Hawkesbury.
Have all these dredges that the hon. gentleman mentioned as being in the maritime provinces actually been at work ?

Yes, I may say that these dredges are not at all sufficient to cope with the work that we should do. I feel that the Public Works Department has not done what it should have done, and that is the reason why I am asking parliament this year for money to build a new suction dredge that will do the work. The port of St. John should be dredged. It is one of our winter ports. Vessels cannot go in and out at every hour of the day. There is.work for eight or ten years for a big suction dredge in the maritime provinces.
Dredge Vessels-Repairs-British Columbia,
That is to pay for the work on the dredges.
The usual vote?

Yes.
New Dredging Plant-Ontario and Quebec, $75,-
000.
Would the hon. gentleman make a statement as to how these dredges are getting on that he started so long ago ?

We are building a powerful elevator dredge at Sorel for the province of Ontario. This money will be applied for that. I intend asking parliament for another amount for a suction dredge. The trade of this country is developing marvellously, the shipping on the lakes is increasing and as, unfortunately, nearly all our harbours are shallow, unles we provide more depth immediately we will lose our trade. I will lay on the Table of the House a statement of all the calls that are made on us for dredging. This is not a party question, and I ask the support of members of parliament to help me and to help themselves, of course.
I understand the suction dredge is for the St. Lawrence.

This is the elevator dredge. Our dredges in Ontario are inferior and simply waste money. I will ask parliament to grant me

money to build a suction dredge to be used in Ontario exclusively.
Can the suction dredge be constructed in this country ?

Most decidedly. I ask my friends on both sides of the House to visit the shipyard in Sorel. I have been severely criticised for having built a shipyard there, but we are training men who will be able to build not only dredges but ships, and although we may not be able to do it in all cases we should build our ships there as well. I make bold to say that the elevator dredges that we built at Sorel are the best of their kind in America. We have benefited by the experience of the American builders and I have to-day the services of Mr. Robinson, a Canadian, formerly an employee of the Montreal Harbour Commission, who for years was consulting engineer for some of the greatest works carried out in the United States. He has supervised the building of 120 dredges. We have availed ourselves of his services to supervise the dredges now being built at the Poison Works at Toronto and he is also helping us at Sorel. I have good men at Sorel. Mr. Howden, the superintendent, is a very capable man. He is not a highly educated man, but I have been told by those most competent to judge that Mr. Howden has invented pieces of machinery that are not to be found elsewhere. Experience is a great educator indeed.

What is the mode of operation of these suction dredges ?
The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS There is vast machinery inside the dredge and on the American dredges there is a pipe at the front, but we are going to put the pipe in the centre of the hull so as to be able to handle it with more ease. At the end of that pipe there will be a. rotary knife which cuts the material, and In the American dredges that material i3 disintegrated with strong jets of water-. The material we have to dredge is a little harder and we propose to use the rotary cutter to better advantage. This cutter, so to speak, provides the food for the dredge. The suction pump takes that material in at the rate of forty feet a minute and the discharge pipes can throw the material to a distance of 3,000 feet. It is almost incredible to imagine this. The big suction pipe dredge we are building at Toronto will be at work on Lake St. Peter by the middle or the end of August next, and we intend discharging the material to a distance of 1,000 feet. Each piece of the discharge pipe will be 90 feet long supported on buoys of about the same length. The discharge pipe will be partially in the water and w'ill be supported by a scow at the end. We expect very great results from these magnificent dredges. We expect to dredge for a cent a yard, but suppose it will cost two cents, it will be revolutionary. I intend
to have one of these dredges for the maritime provinces. Two are under construction at Toronto now, one for British Columbia and the other for the St. Lawrence.
What will they cost ?
The dredge under contract at Toronto will cost $250,000.
Are they let by contract ?
Yes.

I would remind the hon. gentleman of the discussion which took place on this subject last year. Since then, a very important steel shipyard has been undertaken at Collingwood, and it would be a magnificent place at which to get these dredges built. There will be both iron and wood there in unlimited quantities. I think it would be well for the hou. gentleman to look into the situation, and see if he cannot get them built more cheaply there than at Sorel. Besides, it will cost a good deal to bring them up from Sorel. Is the hon. minister building at Sorel the scows for the Georgian Bay and the upper lakes ?

The scows for use on the St. Lawrence will be built at Sorel; but I do not think we shall be able to build at Sorel the dredges for the lakes, as we have our hands full there. I shall be only too glad to inquire from the shipyard people at Collingwood whether they will be in a position to build a dredge for us, and to ask prices from them.

I understand that of the suction dredges building at Toronto, one is for use on the St. Lawrence, and the other in British Columbia. There is a great scarcity of dredging plant on the upper lakes and in the Georgian Bay, and I think it would be wise to provide more plant for them.

I am building at, Sorel an elevator dredge for the upper lakes, and I may say that my colleagues have allowed me to place in the estimates an amount sufficient to build a suction dredge for the lakes.

I want to express my great regret that I do not find anything in the estimates this year for Kingston harbour. 1 am grateful, and so are the people of Kingston, for the money that has been expended on that harbour in the past year ; but when we recognize the existing strife for trade by way of the St. Lawrence, the importance of the harbour of Kingston, and the necessity, as the minister said tonight, of helping those who help themselves, then I do think that some further money should be expended this year in dredging in the harbour of Kingston. The city of Kingston, seeing the necessity of meeting the competition for the trade of the St. Lawrence, has done a great deal to help itself in this matter. In the first place, it bonused to the extent of $20,000 an independent elevator unconnected with any of the transportation companies, but simply for the purpose of affording storing facilities for grain. Then, a transportation company, which, although having its head office at Montreal, has its business centre at Kingston, tried to afford facilities for trade by causing to be built in England two large steamships, one of which has been- in the trade for the last four years, and the other for the last three years, each with a capacity of about 90,000 bushels ; and that company, in connection with its transportation business, and knowing that it was not going to make a single penny in the storage of grain,

but simply as a necessity in the transportation business, built an elevator at a cost of $130,000 ; and to this also the city contributed $35,000. So that in both of these ways the city of Kingston has invested large sums of money with an enterprise which I think does it credit. Now, whatever may be the solution of the transportation problem, I do say that Kingston, situated at the foot of the lakes and at the head of the River St. Lawrence, must be an important point in the trade of the St. Lawrence ; and that being the case, we ought to spend more money, and spend it immediately, to make the harbour of Kingston, not a harbour of refuge, but a harbour for the receiving of grain which is to be transhipped there and taken down the St. Lawrence. I find in the estimates an item of $22,000 to afford facilities to connect the Central Ontario Railway with the docks at the town of Trenton. I do not object to that ; I suppose it is necessary ; but when I see that amount for the little town of Trenton, I only regret that the minister has not seen his way clear to put a vote in the estimates this year for Kingston. I put this plea forward as to the importance of Kingston, and because Kingston has helped itself in the way I have mentioned ; and 1 hope that the minister will see, as the people of Kingston do, the necessity of spending more money there, to make the harbour as complete as possible for the purposes of trade.

If we want men back we generally make an examination among those whom we have employed and who were good men.

Many people are inclined, are uncharitable enough to believe that the hon. gentleman dismissed these people in order that he might put others in their places. It would be only just to these men that they should be taken back when their places require to be filled.

Nothing gives me greater pain than to dismiss men, but on the other hand, this is not a charitable institution. At times all Ministers of Public Works have had to yield to public pressure. The position of the Minister of Public Works is by no means a comfortable one. There is no department in which there is more trouble, and I wish that some abler man had taken hold of it when this government was formed.
How many did the hon. gentleman dismiss ?
About 45 or 50-15 mechanical, 25 labourers and 10 or 12 painters.
How came the hon. gentleman to make a raid on the mechanical department ?	[DOT]

It had become too large. There was no special raid on that department. During the last three or four months I have dismissed 100. Mr. Ewart is chief architect. He asks the heads of the different branches to report the number of men they want and the number they can dispense with. On their reports I dismiss the men we do not require.
The chief of the mechanical department is Mr. King. It was on his report that 15 men were dismissed. The head of the painters is Mr. Cote and the head of the labouring men is Mr. Breton. It is on their report that those dismissals were made.
Do not the reports contain the names of the men ?

I called Mr. Ewart in and asked him how many men he wanted to keep. I said to him : Do not make any party politics, but keep the best men.

I desire to make a short statement and an appeal to the Minister of Public Works with reference to a matter that has been hanging fire for a couple of years. I think the House will sanction the minister in paying the amount. Before the drill hall in Kingston was located, an architect of unquestionable repute and ability was asked by the district officer commanding there to look at the different sites owned by the government, and make some measurements, and be ready to assist in locating the site when the minister came from Ottawa.
Who was the district officer commanding.

Col. Montizambert. The minister made his visit, and, in company with several of the military men, and a number of other gentlemen in Kingston, visited the different properties owned by the government. The architect to whom I have referred made measurements and a rough plan. Afterwards, when it was decided to erect an armouries building, the plans were made by the architect in the minister's department in Ottawa. When the building was being erected, a superintendent of works was employed, but it was not the architect to whom I have referred. This gentleman has moved away from Kingston and is living in British Columbia. His wile still re'sides in Kingston. A bill was rendered by him for his services in making the rough plans, taking the measurements, &e. The bill is a moderate one in my opinion, and in the opinion of architects. But a difficulty has arisen like this-the minister says : I cannot recognize this account unless it is recommended by the Minister of Militia ; and the Minister of Militia says that he never authorized the work, and that his department knew nothing about the work done by Mr. Newlands-that is the gentleman's name-and so he cannot authorize the account to be paid. Here was a

work actually done. Some benefit was derived by the government from the work, because to build properly, it was necessary to have measurements of the sites and rough plans of the building that could be erected on one'or other of these different sites. I make this appeal in Committee of the Whole to the minister on behalf of Mr. Newlands. He is no longer in the province and cannot attend here in Ottawa to urge his claim. His family have not yet removed out of the province. Of course, it would be no argument to say that the person making the claim is in need of the money, and I do not know that I should be authorized to say that. But I say that knowing what he did it seems a just and fair claim, and I regret that I have not been able to get the Minister of Militia to recommend it or the Minister of Public Works to recognize it without that recommendation. All I can do is to say as I am saying now- and it cannot be fairly contradicted it seems to me-that this money has been earned by this architect, and ought to be paid. If there was no authorization, there was at least recognition by the minister going to these sites and doing what he did. The amount of the claim is $125. I think the sum is reasonable. But, if not. then some sum that is reasonable ought to be paid. I ask the hon. minister to look into this matter, and put in an item into the supplementary estimates to pay this claim.

I quite admit that it is a meritorious case. I have looked into the matter myself. There is evidence that Mr. Newlands was asked by Col. Montizambert to look over the sites and prepare plans. Col. Montizambert was in no way employed by the Department of Public Works, in no way connected with that department. Lacking that connection, I cannot see that I would be justified in putting the amount in the estimates. But if my hon. friend the lion. Minister of Militia (Hon. Mr. Borden) were in his seat, I think he would be convinced by the statement my hon. friend has just made. And I would invite him to go again to interview the Minister of Militia. 1 shall be ready to abide by the decision of my colleague.
